literature.title: Fundamental Research Applied To Enable Hardware Performance in Microgravity
literature.link_rule: 'DAFT' + combustion term in title/abstract
literature.abstract: NASA sponsors microgravity research to generate knowledge in physical sciences. In some cases, that knowledge must be applied to enable future research. This article describes one such example. The Dust and Aerosol measurement Feasibility Test (DAFT) is a risk-mitigation experiment developed at the NASA Glenn Research Center by NASA and ZIN Technologies, Inc., in support of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME). SAME is an investigation that is being designed for operation in the Microgravity Science Glovebox aboard the International Space Station (ISS). The purpose of DAFT is to evaluate the performance of P-Trak (TSI Incorporated, Shoreview, MN)--a commercially available condensation nuclei counter and a key SAME diagnostic- -in long-duration microgravity because of concerns about its ability to operate properly in that environment. If its microgravity performance is proven, this device will advance the state of the art in particle measurement capabilities for space vehicles and facilities, such as aboard the ISS. The P-Trak, a hand-held instrument, can count individual particles as small as 20 nm in diameter in an aerosol stream. Particles are drawn into the device by a built-in suction pump. Upon entering the instrument, these particles pass through a saturator tube where they mix with an alcohol vapor (see the following figure). This mixture then flows through a cooled condenser tube where some of the alcohol condenses onto the sample particles, and the droplets grow in a controlled fashion until they are large enough to be counted. These larger droplets pass through an internal nozzle and past a focused laser beam, producing flashes of light that are sensed by a photodetector and then counted to determine particle number concentration. The operation of the instrument depends on the proper internal flow and recycling of isopropyl alcohol in both the vapor and liquid phases.

title.value: DEvice for the study of Critical LIquids and Crystallization Directional Solidification Insert-Reflight

objectives.value: The main objective of the DSI-R investigation was to quantitatively establish the fundamental physics controlling the spatiotemporal organization of the secondary sidebranch structure and its interaction with the array structure of primary branches under directional solidification conditions. This investigation particularly focused on the origin of sidebranches that occur when columnar solidification patterns transform from cellular to dendritic as a function of thermal gradient and solidification velocity and study the potential for the formation of an intermediate multiplet pattern. The dynamics and stability of cellular and dendritic growth patterns, and the relationship between the tip geometry and growth pattern were also to be investigated as well. This intent of this investigation was to directly address outstanding issues that remain open in the understanding of complex dendritic microstructures.

approach.value: The DSI-R investigation utilized a Bridgman type furnace and an experimental cartridge containing the organic transparent alloy of succinonitrile (SCN) - camphor. The nominal concentration was 0.46 wt% camphor. A single crystalline solid seed with a 100 direction parallel to the pulling axial direction is kept unmelted during all experiments.  Solidification is performed by pulling the experimental cartridge containing the alloy inside a thermal gradient G at a pulling rate V. The G and V were the primary variable for each experimental run. Images obtained by the direct axial observation, providing top-view interface images, and transverse observations, providing side-view interface images, were analyzed.

hypothesis.value:
Bridgman solidification of transparent binary alloys in a diffusion controlled growth regime can yield benchmark data required for establishing the detailed dynamics of interface pattern selection.

The ''SPAtiotemporal evolution of three-dimensional DEndritic array Structures'' (SPADES) investigation conducted during the reflight of the Directional Solidification Insert (DSI-R) campaign targeted the columnar dendritic growth regime to quantitatively establish the fundamental physics controlling the spatiotemporal organization of the secondary sidebranch structure and its interaction with the array structure of primary branches under directional solidification conditions.

SPADES focused on the origin of sidebranches that occur when columnar solidification patterns transform from cellular to dendritic as a function of thermal gradient and solidification velocity.

The “Effects of Curvature and Unsteady Dynamics on Alloy Solidification Patterns” (CUSP) investigation extended the DSIP and SPADES project into a new direction that addressed the critical effects of the macroscopic curvature of the solidification front and the unsteady dynamics that occurs in response to changes of growth conditions or that is associated with side-branching.

A weak macroscopic interface curvature can have a major effect on both the array pattern evolution and grain structure. The convex and concave interfaces lead to a continuous increase and decrease  of the average primary spacing, respectively, and it only attains a stationary value for a flat interface.

research_impacts.value: By providing a reduced gravity environment where fluid convection is suppressed, space enables the direct experimental observation of the solid-liquid interface dynamics during the solidification process under long-duration and purely diffusive conditions. The acquired benchmark data will make it uniquely possible to critically test computational models of alloy microstructures by quantitative comparisons of modeling predictions and experimental observations, thereby contributing to the development of Integrated Computational Materials and Engineering (ICME) tools for both space and earth applications. Those tools are expected to “shorten development time, optimize designs and reduce costs relative to more traditional strategies involving building prototypes, testing and redesigning philosophies. In addition, understanding alloy solidification in the microgravity environment of space is important to improve in-space processing (manufacturing, joining, and welding) of structural materials that will be used for future space exploration.

title.value: DEvice for the study of Critical LIquids and Crystallization - Alice Like Insert

objectives.value:
Identify and clarify the different growth mechanisms in fluid systems where hydrodynamics is relevant, particularly during phase separation near the critical point.

To investigate the role of fluctuating hydrodynamics (Brownian motion and local hydrodynamic interactions) in the coarsening of domains, especially when the equilibrium volume fraction of the new phase is minimal.

To analyze the growth kinetics of new experiments performed at very low volume fractions, taking into account fluctuation relaxation effects and Brownian motion within a hydrodynamic framework.

To investigate phase transitions induced by mechanical quenches (density variations using a piston), a novel approach contrasting with traditional temperature quenches.

To study the phase transition kinetics when the fluid is submitted to external vibration in low-g.

approach.value: The investigation approach for DECLIC-ALI centers on conducting experiments within the microgravity environment of the ISS, utilizing the DECLIC facility and its specialized Alice-Like Insert (ALI, ALI-R, and ALI-2). The approach involves precise control of the temperature and density of the SF6 sample, including temperature and mechanical quenches, as well as heat pulse techniques. A suite of optical diagnostics (Interferometry, shadowgraphy, light scattering, and direct observation) is used to visualize and quantify the SF6 fluid behavior. Different sample cell configurations, including fixed and variable volume cells, are employed within the ALI insert. Data acquisition is performed at high frequencies, and the data are analyzed quantitatively, with a strong emphasis on comparing experimental results with theoretical predictions. The overall approach is iterative, building upon previous space-based experiments and refining both experimental techniques and theoretical models, all focused on understanding the critical phenomena of SF6.

hypothesis.value: It is hypothesized that fluctuating hydrodynamics will dominate domain growth at low volume fractions, challenging classical theories. A sharp transition between growth regimes is expected. Mechanical quenches are hypothesized to be a viable method for inducing phase ordering. The vapor recoil force is believed to significantly influence bubble dynamics and wetting near the critical point. Adiabatic volume changes are expected to reveal the dynamics of the Piston Effect. Critical water is hypothesized to follow the same universality class, and external vibration will affect the dynamics.

research_impacts.value: The DECLIC facility provides power, communications, command, control, data storage, and multiple, flexible optical capabilities in support of each experiment. The knowledge gained will assist in the understanding of the behavior of cryogenic (of or relating to very low temperatures) rocket propellants for the study of dynamics regarding near-ambient temperature critical fluids. DECLIC is designed for telescience from the ground and will offer scientists the capability to remotely control experiment conditions onboard the ISS provided by DECLIC lockers. The use of near-critical fluids allows important parameters (e.g., compressibility of supercritical fluids, density of gas and liquid phases, surface tension) to be easily varied in a scaled way by using small changes in temperature. The readily variable properties of near-critical fluids makes them appealing candidates for studying numerous interesting phenomena valid for all fluids, which will ultimately leads to the development of improved solvents for chemistry and the environment.

title.value: Development and Verification of a 3D Nucleate Pool Boiling Simulation Model Using PSI Data

objectives.value: The primary objective of this investigation was to develop and validate a numerical model for further investigation of nucleate pool boiling problems under microgravity conditions.

approach.value:
The moment-of-fluid (MOF) procedure is employed to reconstruct the interfaces of any number of material interfaces in a computational cell. The salient features of the overall approach includes:
(i) Multi-material interfaces are represented by the piecewise linear moment-of-fluid (MOF) reconstruction, (ii)  the time derivative part of the heat equation is discretized using the backward Euler method which is a discrete maximum principle preserving time discretization scheme, (iii) the spatial derivatives part of the heat equation is discretized using the finite volume method, (iv) the temperature field is discretized on a multi-material “supermesh” in which there is just one temperature variable per material per cell, (v) the discrete location for a given variable is at the materials' centroid, (vi) “connected centroid” method is used in order to approximate fluxes, (vii) at Dirichlet or Neumann embedded interfaces,  a linear exact correction term is prescribed so that the method approximates the temperature gradient with second order accuracy.

hypothesis.value: It is hypothesized that the developed model will have the following advantages which can lead to a more accurate prediction: (1) the method can better resolve thermal boundary layers (away from triple points) using adaptive mesh refinement, (2) a novel Moment of Fluid multiphase flow algorithm will  straightforwardly prescribe a microlayer model in 3D general geometries, (3) the moment of fluid interface capturing algorithm will enable better handling of 3D problems such as bubble merging, (4) the modeling method can better conserve the boiling mass flow rate by directly exploiting the moment-of-fluid (sharp) interface reconstruction for approximating the interface heat flux in the vicinity of multiple (greater than 2) materials.

research_impacts.value: The verified model can be used to further study scenarios not investigated on ISS such as vapor bubble departure and collapse. It can also be used to identify optimal heated surface configuration for better heat transfer characteristics. In addition, the model can be used to study other problems under microgravity such as packed bed reactors. The development of nucleate pool boiling simulation tool in microgravity based on the Navier-Stokes equations from this proposed work can be used to study other boiling problems in Earth gravity such as engine cooling and cooling in electronic devices.

title.value: Electromagnetic Levitation Flight Support for Transient Observation of Nucleation Events

objectives.value:
The objective of this project is to understand phase selection in structural alloys and to investigate the effects of convection on time-dependent nucleation phenomena during rapid solidification from the melt.  The ELFSTONE investigation involves a collaboration with the European Space Agency's (ESA) Thermolab Experiment which focuses on thermophysical properties data measurement of industrial alloys in the liquid phase as a function of temperature. The property values obtained are used to increase the accuracy of numerical modeling of casting and solidification processes of metal alloys.
For access to data relating to the Thermolab Experiment, please consult ESA's HRE Data Archive (hreda.esac.esa.int)

approach.value: The samples are processed in the Electromagnetic Levitator (ISS-EML), a facility that has been operational since 2015 and is located in the Columbus module. The investigation is part of Sample Batch 1 - the first of six proposed 18-sample multi-user cartridges uploaded to the ISS.  For the ELFSTONE Sample #09, a ternary FeCrNi analog steel sample, a process cycle is defined as (1) the melting of the sample, (2) the gathering of science data, and (3) the subsequent undercooling and rapid solidification of the sample. The next cycle starts with the re-melting of the sample.  In any particular cycle, stirring may be induced at different levels to study the effect of convection on rapid solidification behavior.  After all cycles are complete, final microstructure is preserved for return to earth.

hypothesis.value: The experimental hypothesis was that melt convection would significantly decrease the nucleation kinetics for transformation of metastable ferrite to stable austenite in ferrous structural steel alloys. The was successfully observed.

research_impacts.value: The value of this research is that the results have application to the design of industrial welding, spray forming, and casting operations for a commercially important class of structural materials. In addition, this research addresses fundamental issues relating to rapid solidification behavior, metastable phase selection, and analysis of the processes governing microstructural evolution. Experiments focus on the use of convection as a processing control parameter.

title.value: Advanced Colloids Experiment - Temperature Control and Gradient Sample 11

objectives.value: ACE-T11 studies the design and assembly of complex 3D structures from small particles suspended within a fluid medium with control of particle density, phase and behavior.  Objectives included study of nucleation and growth of crystals within colloidal samples by varying the size and concentration of colloids and depletant, exploring the effect of temperature gradients, and demonstrating control of particle shape and density which is essential for creating high performance materials for 3D printing and advanced optical materials.  The research goal is to produce various colloidal structures and study the dynamics of crystal nucleation and growth. The imaging goal is to observe crystallites and resolve particle centroid positions with less than 20% error.

approach.value: The ACE-T11 investigation used 2 Sample Modules (SM), each containing 3 capillary cells for a total of 6 samples. Confocal microscopy was employed for 3D imaging of non-spherical colloids, with phases controlled by adding depletants, adjusting spatial temperature changes, and applying temperature gradients. The size and concentration of both the particles and depletants were varied across different samples. After homogenization using a magnetic stirrer, the particles were left undisturbed to crystallize. Preliminary observations were made with a 2.5X objective, followed by detailed imaging using 10X, 63X, and 100X objectives.

hypothesis.value: Under microgravity conditions, colloidal particles would exhibit unique crystallization and self-assembly behaviors that differ from those observed under Earth's gravity. Researchers believed that without the effects of sedimentation, they would better understand the fundamental mechanisms governing colloidal phase transitions and self-organization​.  This hypothesis also included the idea that controlling external factors like temperature and depletant concentration would enable precise manipulation of colloidal structures, allowing for the creation of more complex and functional materials.

research_impacts.value:
Future space missions will require self-assembly and self-replication technologies for self-repairing materials and devices, essential for long-duration travel. 3D printing and additive manufacturing are crucial for creating replacement parts, with research focusing on developing particle slurries and pastes suited for both micro and regular gravity environments.
This research advances soft matter science, with applications in medicine, electronics, and photonics. Self-assembly techniques will enable new devices for energy and communication, while 3D printing and additive manufacturing rely on optimizing high-density slurries and pastes with diverse mechanical properties.

title.value: Capillary Channel Flow - Critical Velocities Experiment Unit 1

objectives.value: The investigation aims to characterize and quantify critical flow dynamics in open capillary channels of parallel plate and groove geometries. A primary objective is determining the critical flow rates at which free surface destabilization (''choking'') and gas ingestion occur, emphasizing the capillary-inertial regime. The investigation will examine the relationship between critical flow rate and channel length for complete and half-channel configurations. Controlled, low-frequency flow oscillations will be introduced to probe instability onset sensitivity across geometries and lengths. High-fidelity data on free surface shapes and critical velocities will be acquired to validate theoretical models and assess underlying assumptions, refining predictive capabilities for capillary flows relevant to spacecraft fluid management.

approach.value: The CCF experiment was operated on the ISS in the MSG. The CCF hardware consists of two experiment units, experiment unit number #1 for the parallel plate and groove geometry, and experiment unit number #2 for the wedge geometry. Initally, one experiment campaign for each experiment unit was planned. Due to the great success of the first two runs, two more additional runs were performed. The challenge for these runs was the commissioning of the fluid loop. The original design of the hardware did not foresee a commissioning from an undefined state, as it was the case after the first operation of each module. The fluid management technology builtinto the CCF hardware - however - was able to recover from an undefined fluid distribution state and allowed additional runs.

hypothesis.value: The primary hypothesis guiding CCF-CV EU1 is that a limiting flow rate, or 'choking' phenomenon, exists in open capillary channels with parallel plate and groove geometries. A relationship between the fluid velocity, the channel geometry, and the fluid properties governs this limit. Furthermore, it is hypothesized that the introduction of wave oscillations within the flow will impact the critical flow rate, with the amplitude and frequency of these oscillations playing a significant role in the flow behavior and the onset of choking.

research_impacts.value:
The knowledge of liquid management in space is important for any device which contain liquid and gas, and have one or many free liquid surfaces. The requirements for the device which experiences different acceleration levels down to fully compensated gravity conditions (weightlessness) during its operation may include the phase separation of liquid from gas, gas from liquid, and the transport of liquid through liquid acquisition devices. The results from the CCF experiments may help to design subsystems of future spacecrafts, such as the propulsion subsystem, the thermal control subsystem and the life support subsystem for crewed exploration. The data can be used to build mathematical models which can be applied to real fluids and real dimensions. The data can be used as well to validate computational fluid dynamics software packages which are state-of-the-art tools the design of spacecrafts.
Capillary forces on Earth are masked by gravity, but may become dominant in small scales. This can be encountered when a wetting liquid wicks into a porous structure. title.value: Capillary Channel Flow - Critical Velocities Experiment Unit 2

objectives.value: The investigation aims to determine critical flow rates (choking) for wedge channels across various lengths and wedge angles. It explores choking behavior across capillary-inertial, visco-capillary, and overlap flow regimes. Bubble transport, migration, and phase separation within wedge geometries will also be investigated, focusing on the influence of flow rate, channel length, and bubble diameter.

approach.value: The CCF experiment was operated on the ISS in the MSG. The CCF hardware consists of two experiment units, experiment unit number #1 for the parallel plate and groove geometry, and experiment unit number #2 for the wedge geometry. Initially, one experiment campaign for each experiment unit was planned. Due to the great success of the first two runs, two more additional runs were performed. The challenge for these runs was the commissioning of the fluid loop. The original design of the hardware did not foresee a commissioning from an undefined state, as it was the case after the first operation of each module. The fluid management technology built into the CCF hardware - however - was able to recover from an undefined fluid distribution state and allowed additional runs.

hypothesis.value: The central hypothesis for CCF-CV EU2 is that a critical flow rate limit also exists in open capillary channels with wedge and gapped-wedge geometries, and it is governed by the interplay of capillary, viscous, and inertial forces. It is expected that the critical flow rate will be a function of the channel geometry, which includes the wedge angle and channel length, and that there will be different flow regimes which are linked to the governing flow forces. Furthermore, it is hypothesized that the nature of bubble transport, migration, and phase separation will depend on the flow conditions, such as flow rate and channel length, as well as bubble properties, such as the size and frequency.

title.value: Capillary Channel Flow - Phase Separation Experiment Unit 2

objectives.value: The objectives are to quantify phase separation efficiency in wedge channels as a function of flow parameters, bubble characteristics, and channel geometry; determine the influence of bubble size and injection frequency on separation efficiency; and optimize wedge geometry for passive phase separation.

approach.value: Building upon the CF-CV EU2 approach, the phase separation investigation utilizes a controlled bubble injection system to introduce bubbles of varying sizes and frequencies upstream of the wedge channel. The microgravity environment of the ISS ensures capillary-dominated flow conditions. Systematic variation of bubble injection parameters (size, frequency, location), flow rate, and channel geometry (wedge angle, length) enables comprehensive mapping of phase separation efficiency. High-speed imaging (HSHRC) coupled with wider-view video (MSGC) allows for detailed observation and quantification of bubble migration and coalescence. Image analysis techniques are employed to track bubble trajectories, quantify bubble size distributions before and after the wedge channel, and determine the overall degree of gas-liquid separation. This quantitative data is then correlated with the varied parameters to assess the effectiveness of the wedge geometry for passive phase separation and to optimize design parameters for enhanced performance.

hypothesis.value: The hypothesis underlying CCF-PS EU2 is that specific wedge and gapped-wedge channel designs can passively separate liquid and gas phases due to the complex interplay of capillary and inertial forces. Furthermore, it is hypothesized that by carefully adjusting flow conditions, such as flow rate and channel length as well as bubble properties, such as bubble size and frequency, it is possible to identify geometries and regimes suitable for gas-liquid separation, which can be used for spacecraft tank design and liquid supply.

research_impacts.value: Current spacecraft fuel tanks rely on an additional reservoir to prevent gases from entering the engines during firing. Capillary systems larger than a few millimeters in length are impossible to study on the ground, but the weightlessness on the International Space Station makes research on a variety of capillary channel sizes possible. The results are useful for the design and testing of liquid management systems in current use and for future missions. Rocket fuel tank designs and construction models from space research help to advance new technology and manufacturing capabilities on Earth.

title.value: Computational and Experimental Analysis of SPICE Data Sets

objectives.value: This ground investigation  sought to increase understanding of the issues that control the large discrepancy between soot formation in 1g and in 0g flames.  The objective of this investigation was to integrate computational and experimental methods to derive temperature distributions and soot volume fractions from the Smoke Point in Coflow Experiment (SPICE) data available in PSI. By analyzing over 1600 raw DSLR images and incorporating advanced soot models, the study sought to improve understanding of soot formation, oxidation, radiative re-absorption, and aggregate growth in heavily sooting flames. The work further aimed to reconcile microgravity and normal gravity flame behavior, identify key physical and chemical processes influencing smoke point development, and provide a framework for evaluating model parameter sensitivity.

approach.value: The approach  was to combine image processing, experimental diagnostics, and detailed soot modeling. Raw Nikon NEF images were decoded into three color channels and analyzed using color-ratio pyrometry to extract soot temperature fields. Absolute light calibration from SPICE was then used to calculate soot volume fractions. For computational modeling, a coupled flow–species–soot system was implemented, modified to include radiation re-absorption and discrete-sectional aggregate formation. Simulations were performed for both Yale and ACME burner configurations under normal and microgravity conditions. Comparisons between experimental data and computed results guided sensitivity analyses of soot evolution parameters, including the effects of radiation, scattering, boundary conditions, and heat transfer to the burner structure.

hypothesis.value: Microgravity conditions would produce longer, more diffuse flames with lower temperatures and increased soot concentrations compared to normal gravity, and that careful integration of experimental temperature fields into the simulations would reduce discrepancies between measured and predicted soot distributions.

research_impacts.value: This study sought to enhance understanding of soot formation, flame structure, and radiative transport under microgravity and normal gravity, improving predictive models for combustion in both spacecraft and terrestrial systems. For space applications, the results support safer fire detection, suppression, and cleaner combustion technologies critical for long-duration missions. On Earth, the insights help reduce pollutant emissions, optimize combustion efficiency, and inform the design of cleaner energy and industrial systems.

title.value: Concurrent Flame Spread Modeling using Flamelet Generated Manifolds in Microgravity with Comparison to BASS Experiments using Two-Color Tomography

objectives.value:
The objective of this research was to develop and validate new flamelet generated manifold (FGM) modeling techniques for concurrent flame spread in microgravity. Concurrent flame spread presented one of the greatest modeling challenges in combustion science due to the intricate coupling between heat transfer, mass transport, and chemical kinetics near the solid-vapor interface. Traditional modeling strategies often relied on hybridized turbulence and chemistry models that were not fully consistent and failed to capture important intermediate reaction pathways.
To overcome these shortcomings, this PSI grant advanced the use of an unsteady flamelet generated manifold (UFGM) framework that reduced the complexity of reacting systems by mapping them into lower-dimensional manifolds. The research aimed to leverage this methodology to simulate solid fuel combustion processes with high fidelity, using the NASA Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS and BASS-II) experiments as benchmarks. Ultimately, the long-term goal was to enable accurate prediction of flammability limits for spacecraft materials and to provide a tool that could also serve as a subgrid-scale model in large-eddy simulations of fires, supporting spacecraft safety and hazard mitigation.

approach.value:
The approach combined high-resolution computational modeling with experimental validation to study concurrent flame spread in microgravity. A previously developed computational framework  was employed to run fully coupled simulations of fluid–solid responses, focusing on materials subject to charring and ablation. Within this framework, the unsteady FGM method was implemented and tested on various BASS geometries, including flat sheets, spheres, and rod-shaped polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) samples, as well as wax cylinders.
Experimental imagery found in PSI from the BASS and BASS-II investigations was post-processed using newly developed two-color tomography methods with DSLR cameras, enabling 3D reconstructions of soot and temperature fields for direct comparison to model predictions. The evaluation metrics included flame geometry, temperature distribution, soot volume fraction, and flame spread rate, with special emphasis on reproducing the “Goldilocks” flammability zone reported by Olson and Ferkul. Comparative analyses were also carried out with a parallel NSF-supported terrestrial flame spread project, ensuring that the predictive capabilities of the UFGM approach were assessed across both microgravity and normal-gravity conditions.

hypothesis.value: The unsteady flamelet generated manifold (UFGM) approach was believed to be able to accurately reproduce concurrent flame spread in microgravity, including phenomena such as the “Goldilocks” flammability zone, by coupling near-wall thermal, mass transport, and chemical processes with far-field flow dynamics.

research_impacts.value: This research provides predictive tools for screening new materials’ flammability limits, which can lead to the design of safer spacecrafts. The development of Large Eddy Simulation subgrid models is expected to improve hazard assessment capabilities critical for managing fire risks during long-duration space missions and within confined spacecraft habitats. On Earth, these advancements could improve combustion modeling by deepening our understanding of coupled thermal, chemical, and flow processes, which betters fire safety standards. The computational methods being refined have the potential to enable more effective fire prevention and mitigation strategies and  foster innovations in diagnostics and simulations applicable across a variety of combustion scenarios. Overall, this research can contribute significantly to safer human exploration in space and improvements to fire safety protocols on Earth.

title.value: DEvice for the study of Critical LIquids and Crystallization - Directional Solidification Insert

objectives.value: The objective of this investigation was to obtain benchmark data on cellular and dendritic growth under diffusive growth conditions. Precise measurements of interface shape, cell/dendrite tip radius, tip composition and tip temperature will be carried out as a function of composition, growth rate and thermal gradient values.  By systematically varying the process parameters in the absence of gravity-induced convection, the range of interface morphologies will be obtained, yielding insight into the underlying principles that govern dynamical pattern selection. Directional solidification experiments conducted in microgravity using transparent organic analogues will provide real time benchmark data to quantitatively determine conditions for the planar to cellular and cell to dendrite transitions and validate a predictive phase field 3D being developed as part of the investigation.

approach.value: Experiments were performed within the Directional Solidification Insert (DSI) of the Device for the study of Critical LIquids and Crystallization (DECLIC) aboard the International Space Station. Homogeneous 3D cylindrical samples in a classical Bridgman setup was processed with various pulling velocities V and temperature gradients G. The transparent succinonitrile (SCN)-0.24wt% camphor alloy was the sample material and it permitted in situ optical imaging of the solid/liquid interface. Experiments were typically initiated from a single crystal growing along the temperature gradient direction. The alloy solidified within a cylindrical crucible with an inner diameter of 10mm. The solid/liquid interface was located within a stable and well-controlled temperature gradient. The crucible was pulled through an axial adiabatic zone, allowing the interface to grow up to 100 mm in length at a controlled velocity. While independently controlling V and  G experienced by the interface, in situ evolution of the solid/liquid interface morphology was imaged and analyzed. 3D phase-field simulations were specifically developed to identify ranges of primary spacings for the formation of the classically observed “fingers” (deep cells) with blunt tips and “needles” with parabolic tips.

hypothesis.value: When a planar solid-liquid becomes unstable, under certain growth conditions, complex interactions among perturbed regions can lead to different amplification rates of different wavelengths that determines the final selection of the reorganized pattern. This complex dynamical process selects a small range of wavelengths, from an unstable spectrum of wavelengths, to form a periodic array of cells.

research_impacts.value: From the technological viewpoint, the importance of cellular and dendritic microstructures is quite clear since these structures are exhibited in all important commercial solidification techniques. The proposed project will for the first time provide benchmark data for the dynamical evolution of three-dimensional cellular and dendritic patterns that will enable precise modeling of complex commercial processing technologies to give reliable products. The development of a reliable model will allow industries to design new materials and processing conditions that will have a significant impact on the economy in the US, since casting and welding industries are several billion dollars industries. In addition, the fundamental knowledge of pattern formation will allow the development of nano-scale patterns in polymers and electronic materials that will have significant impact on the development of high technology and advanced materials.

title.value: Dynamic Response of Particle-Filled Polymeric Fluids in Flows with Complex Lagrangian Time Histories

objectives.value: The primary objective of this ground investigation is to exploit the unique flight data from the Shear History Extensional Rheology (SHERE, SHERE-II, SHERE-R) investigations to better understand the dynamic rheology of particle-filled polymeric fluids in complex flows. These fluids, encountered in manufacturing processes such as fiber spinning, hydraulic fracturing, and roll-to-roll film production, experience alternating regimes of shear and extension in a Lagrangian frame. By using SHERE’s microgravity dataset, the study seeks to isolate the interplay between polymer stresses, particle orientation, and flow disturbances—effects that cannot be cleanly separated in Earth’s gravity. The overarching goal is to develop quantitative predictions and mechanistic insights into how particles alter extensional flow responses, strain hardening, and energy dissipation in viscoelastic suspensions.

approach.value: The investigation combines numerical simulations, theoretical modeling, and SHERE flight data validation. The SHERE experiments measured transient extensional responses of dilute particle suspensions in Boger fluids at moderate extension rates—regimes inaccessible on Earth due to sedimentation and buoyancy. To interpret these data, the project applies finite-difference methods in spheroidal coordinates to resolve inertia-less viscoelastic flows around suspended particles, capturing strong local stress gradients near particle surfaces. Semi-analytical theories are also employed to predict rheology in the limit of small polymer concentrations, allowing parameter sweeps that are computationally prohibitive in full simulations. Three flow classes are studied: (1) sphere suspensions in transient extension with/without pre-shear to directly compare with SHERE data; (2) spheroidal particle suspensions transitioning between shear and extension to mimic fiber-film processing; and (3) alternating shear/extension flows modeling turbulent drag reduction. Together, this multi-method approach bridges PSI experimental data with first-principles rheological predictions.

hypothesis.value: The central hypothesis is that particle-polymer interactions fundamentally alter the transient extensional rheology of polymer solutions in ways that cannot be predicted by simple additive models of particle and polymer stresses. Specifically, the particle-induced velocity disturbances are expected to modify local polymer stress distributions, suppress strain hardening at large deformations, and alter stress development depending on flow history (e.g., pre-shear orientation effects). Furthermore, anisotropic particles such as spheroids will introduce orientation-dependent rheological signatures, leading to different stress responses under alternating shear and extension. By validating these predictions with SHERE microgravity data, the study tests whether advanced numerical and theoretical models can accurately capture the coupled dynamics of particles and polymers across relevant industrial flow regimes.

research_impacts.value:
In-Space Benefits: For space exploration and on-orbit manufacturing, understanding the rheology of particle-laden polymeric fluids is crucial for the design of efficient life-support systems, in-space fabrication, and thermal management technologies. Microgravity eliminates sedimentation, enabling stable suspensions and novel material processing methods, such as fiber spinning and advanced coatings. Insights from SHERE-based models improve predictability of fluid performance in spacecraft systems where multiphase, particle-laden fluids may be used.

Earth Benefits: On Earth, particle-polymer suspensions underpin industries such as hydraulic fracturing, fiber spinning, extrusion molding, roll-to-roll manufacturing, and enhanced oil recovery. Adding particles imparts tailored mechanical or conductive properties but also increases energy demands due to altered rheology. This project provides mechanistic predictions for how particle orientation and polymer stress coupling influence flow resistance, helping optimize industrial processes, reduce energy consumption, and enable development of high-performance materials. By combining SHERE microgravity data with advanced modeling, this work addresses gaps in extensional rheology knowledge that hinder efficient design of complex fluid processing systems.

title.value: Enhancement and Verification of Quantitative Phase-Field Crystal Modeling using NASA-PSI Coarsening in Solid- Liquid Mixtures Experiments Data

objectives.value: The key objectives of this investigation were to develop 1) a binary Molecular Dynamics (MD) interatomic potential for Pb-Sn system, 2) Phase Field Crystal (PFC) models for coarsening of solid-liquid mixtures; 3) a highly-parallel semi-implicit spectral and operator splitting numerical algorithm to use on high performance computing facilities that will enable the necessary large-scale PFC simulations (comparable to CSLM data length-scale); (4) Data mining of NASA-PSI Coarsening in Solid-Liquid Mixtures (CSLM), CSLM-2, CSLM-2R, and CSLM-3 experiments and using them in series of simulations in the developed computational tool for enhancement and verification of the proposed modeling framework.

approach.value:
The proposed multi-scale modeling framework is established around two atomistic computational material model of phase-field crystals (PFC) and molecular dynamics (MD). PFC is a unique computational model at diffusive time scale with the capability of simulating solid-liquid processes with atomistic resolutions while MD acts on the time scale of atomistic vibrations.
A novel approach of modified-embedded-atom (MEAM) interatomic potential was adopted to obtain reliable interatomic potentials for Pb-Sn binary systems near or at the melting point (MP). The potentials were used to calculate relevant properties such as latent heat, expansion in melting, liquid structure factor, solid-liquid interface stiffness, solidus and liquidus lines, and solid-liquid interfacial free energy. The kinetics of coarsening in solid-liquid mixtures (Ostwald ripening of solid domains in the liquid phase) was simulated using a one mode phase field crystal (1PFC) model. The simulation results were compared to experimental data previously obtained in a microgravity environment. Simulations were carried out as a function of the difference in chemical potential between Pb and Sn. Please the data layout document (DLD) describing the data organization in folders for each delta chemical potential and underlying files as per temperature of simulation and each time step.

hypothesis.value: Modified-embedded-atom (MEAM) interatomic potential and a one mode phase field crystal (1PFC) model can be utilized to simulate the kinetics of coarsening of solid phases in solid-liquid mixtures.

research_impacts.value: The proposed computational tool verified/quantified based on CSLM data will establish a virtual laboratory that can be used to study coarsening as well as other material processing phenomena on Earth involving with solid-liquid coexistence; e.g., rapid solidification and grain growth. Since computational models are highly repeatable at lower cost, the proposed modeling framework will result in accelerated material process development and certification. Solid-liquid coexistence is the initial step in many manufacturing technologies such as casting, liquid infiltration, and additive manufacturing. Hence, this modeling framework can be used to investigate the relations between these manufacturing processes and the material properties in order to optimize/control the manufacturing processes parameters. In addition, the results of this research will be disseminated to the public in forms of peer-reviewed articles, scientific reports, a project-specific website, and data uploaded to NASA-PSI website.

title.value: Flame Extinguishment Experiment - 2

objectives.value:
The primary goal of the FLEX-2 flight experiments is to extend the results of FLEX-1 to fuels and environmental conditions that mimic real combustor conditions, as well as, provide benchmark experimental data on bi-component droplet combustion over a wide range of initial conditions in order to validate numerical simulations and to develop new theoretical models.

Detailed experimental objectives can be further itemized as:
  1. Investigate the role of liquid-phase mixing on the burning characteristics of bi-component fuel droplets.
  2. Examine the steady and unsteady liquid and gas-phase phenomena in pure fuel combustion.
  3. Study flame extinction mechanisms and their boundaries.
  4. Analyze the soot formation process, including soot volume fraction soot-shell dynamics.
  5. Determine the influence of droplet interactions on the flammability limits and extinction behavior of droplet arrays.
  6. Validate theoretical models of droplet combustion through comprehensive experimental data collection in microgravity environments.

approach.value:
The chamber was filled with the appropriate atmosphere, which was varied in pressure between 0.5 atm to 3.0 atm and O2 concentration between 0.1 to 0.4 mole fraction with the diluent gas making up the balance. A settling time of approximately 2 minutes  elapsed prior to initiating the test in order to ensure that the temperature and pressure of the chamber gases have stabilized. This settling time was followed by the dispensing of a predetermined amount of fuel (based on the target droplet size) onto the support fiber for those tests in which the droplet is not freely deployed. When sufficient fuel has been dispensed the dispensing needles were retracted and a dwell period of at least 10 seconds was allowed for the droplet internal fluid motion induced by deployment to subside. This was then followed by initiating power to the ignitor for a selectable amount of time ranging from 1 second to 5 seconds after which the ignitor was retracted from the field of view. If the flow field is to be generated by translating the droplet then droplet motion would commence at the same time that the ignitor is retracted. A near real-time download of the color camera video was employed in order to verify successful droplet deployment, ignition, and overall progress of the experiment. Pressure and temperature data of the chamber environment was also recorded in near real time.

The overall investigation approach can be summarized as:
  1. Test parameters are determined, including pressure, temperature, fuel mixture, and humidity.
  2. Fill the combustion chamber with the selected gas mixtures.
  3. Deploy the droplet(s) carefully controlling the droplet diameter.
  4. Allow the droplet to stabilize in the microgravity environment.
  5. Ignite the droplet in a uniform and controlled fashion.
  6. Monitor combustions and track flame evolution using high speed photography.
  7. Monitor and adjust experimental conditions as needed.
  8. Analyze data.

The independently varied experimental parameters during FLEX-2 experiments were 1) Fuel type 2) Ambient gas composition 3) Ambient Pressure 4) Droplet initial diameter 5) Droplet translation velocity (and acceleration) 6) Droplet spacing and initial size in a binary linear array.

hypothesis.value: Fairly sophisticated numerical simulations of convective droplet combustion have been developed in the last decade where the key contribution is the inclusion of full Navier-Stokes equations for the gas-phase flow field. However, due to the inherent complexity of the problem, varying degrees of approximations have been made in treating the chemistry, radiation, and the coupling between the gas and liquid phases. The validity of the assumptions or the hypothesis used in these simulation have not been confirmed by using benchmark data. By conducting these experiments in a microgravity environment, the effects of buoyancy are minimized, and the droplet can be characterized only as a function of thermocapillary or solutalcapillary stresses allowing for a clear observation of the fundamental combustion processes,  The present FLEX-2 experiments using bi-component mixtures. In addition, the microgravity environment allows study of such phenomena as the transitions between radiative and diffusive extension of the flame. The primary goal of the flight experiments is to provide benchmark experimental data on bi-component droplet combustion over a wide range of initial conditions that could be used to validate numerical simulations and to develop new theoretical models.

research_impacts.value:
The combustion of liquid fuels is the overwhelming energy source in the transportation sector. Insights gained from these studies can lead to more efficient and cleaner combustion technologies which are crucial for reducing pollution and greenhouse gas emissions. By improving fuel efficiency and developing better fuels, these experiments can contribute to:

  1) More sustainable energy production.
  2) Future combustor designs with minimal carbon footprint, maximum fuel efficiency and less pollutant emissions.
  3) Allow quantitative evaluation of the performance of future fuels in combustors through the development of surrogates (mixtures of pure fuels that simulate the behavior of real fuels).
  4) Validation of jet engine models by engine manufacturers with support from prior droplet results.

literature.abstract: The Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) program is a continuing set of experiments on droplet combustion, performed employing the Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA), inside the chamber of the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), which is located in the Destiny module of the International Space Station (ISS). This report describes the experimental hardware, the diagnostic equipment, the experimental procedures, and the methods of data analysis for FLEX. It also presents the results of the first 284 tests performed. The intent is not to interpret the experimental results but rather to make them available to the entire scientific community for possible future interpretations.

literature.abstract: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus Flame Extinguishment Experiment (MDCA-FLEX) will assess the effectiveness of fire suppressants in microgravity and quantify the effect of different possible crew exploration atmospheres on fire suppression. The goal of this research is to provide definition and direction for large scale fire suppression tests and selection of the fire suppressant for next generation crew exploration vehicles.

title.value: Flame Extinguishment Experiment

objectives.value: The FLEX (Flame Extinguishment Experiment) investigation aims to map the flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity environments, measure the effectiveness of various gaseous fire suppressants such as CO2, He, and SF6, and develop reliable predictive models for combustion limits under reduced gravity conditions. The mission seeks to validate and improve simplified models by incorporating detailed chemical reactions, heat transfer, and material movement, using both space-based data and extensive ground-based tests. Key flight experiment goals include obtaining high-resolution measurements of droplet burning rates, flame extinction behavior, heat radiation, soot levels, and temperature profiles, while systematically analyzing the effects of different ambient conditions and suppressant concentrations. These investigations are essential for advancing the fundamental understanding of combustion processes in microgravity and enhancing fire safety protocols for future space missions.

approach.value:
The FLEX experiments involve igniting and observing the burning behavior of relatively large droplets. A primary objective of the experiments is to determine the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) as a function of ambient pressure and determine how the presence of a suppressant influences the LOI .
The basic outline of the procedure to construct this diagram is as follows:
  1. Select the test pressure (0.5 − 1.5 atm) for the LOI tests.
  2. Select a smaller droplet size (≈ 3 mm)
  3. Select an ambient oxygen mole fraction that, based on ground-based testing, will support droplets burning to completion (as opposed to extinguishing at a finite droplet size).
  4. Perform a droplet combustion test.
  5. Increase the droplet size or repeat the test (if finite extinction diameter at flame extinction observed).
  6. Continue steps 4 and 5 until flame exists for only a short time after ignition (radiative extinction).
  7. Continue steps 4 thru 6 at a decreased ambient oxygen mole fraction.
  8. Continue step 7 to an ambient oxygen mole fraction where the droplet does not ignite.

There were ambient conditions where the extinction droplet sizes at all ambient oxygen mole fractions were too small to either be observed or measured with the available diagnostics. In this case, the determination of the LOI is similar, but more iterative. Instead of observing flame extinction, however, the procedure  involved an iterative sequence of tests (burn to completion followed by a no ignition test) with progressively smaller increments in ambient oxygen mole fraction to determine the LOI . For the slow flow tests (in the flight experiment), the configuration of the flight hardware did not allow for adequate diagnostics over the entire test for a droplet in a uniform, steady convective flow.  In these tests, the procedure will be to duplicate tests above which yield finite-sized extinction droplet diameters. Near the end of the tests, prior to flame extinction, the droplet will be subjected to a small, sub-buoyant, convective flow (imparted by translating the droplet at a slow, uniform speed).

The goal of the experiment is then to see how the presence of this flow influences the extinction process. Note, a large number of the tests involve free droplets (as opposed to fiber-supported droplets) and a number of these tests will have droplets with a slow drift velocity. Data gathered from these tests to examine the influences of a small, sub-buoyant flow on both the burning and extinction process.

hypothesis.value: The primary hypothesis of the FLEX mission is that microgravity conditions fundamentally alter the combustion and extinction characteristics of liquid fuel droplets due to changes in species and energy transport dynamics, radiative heat loss, and chemical kinetics. Specifically, the hypothesis posits that the lack of buoyant convection in microgravity will lead to significant differences in the flammability limits and suppression efficacy of various fire suppressant agents compared to normal gravity conditions. This hypothesis underpins the design of the FLEX experiments, which aim to map flammability boundaries, quantify suppressant efficacy, and develop predictive models to improve fire safety in space environments.

research_impacts.value: The research impacts and Earth benefits of the FLEX mission are significant and multifaceted. By enhancing our understanding of microgravity combustion, the mission directly contributes to improved fire safety protocols for future space missions, ensuring the safety of crew members in environments where traditional fire suppression methods may be ineffective. On Earth, the insights gained from these experiments have the potential to advance fire safety in confined and reduced-gravity environments, such as submarines or high-altitude aircraft. The mission's findings on the effectiveness of various fire suppressants, including CO2, He, and SF6, in microgravity can lead to the development of more efficient and less harmful fire suppression systems, reducing the risk of toxic byproducts during fire events. Additionally, the study of ''cool flames'' and low-temperature combustion processes observed in microgravity can inform the design of advanced combustion engines, leading to improved fuel efficiency and reduced emissions in automotive and industrial applications. Overall, the FLEX mission's contributions to combustion science have the potential to enhance both space exploration safety and terrestrial fire safety technologies.

microgravity.sentence: The FLEX (Flame Extinguishment Experiment) investigation aims to map the flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity environments, measure the effectiveness of various gaseous fire suppressants such as CO2, He, and SF6, and develop reliable predictive models for combustion limits under reduced gravity conditions.
These investigations are essential for advancing the fundamental understanding of combustion processes in microgravity and enhancing fire safety protocols for future space missions.

The primary hypothesis of the FLEX mission is that microgravity conditions fundamentally alter the combustion and extinction characteristics of liquid fuel droplets due to changes in species and energy transport dynamics, radiative heat loss, and chemical kinetics.

Specifically, the hypothesis posits that the lack of buoyant convection in microgravity will lead to significant differences in the flammability limits and suppression efficacy of various fire suppressant agents compared to normal gravity conditions.

By enhancing our understanding of microgravity combustion, the mission directly contributes to improved fire safety protocols for future space missions, ensuring the safety of crew members in environments where traditional fire suppression methods may be ineffective.

The mission's findings on the effectiveness of various fire suppressants, including CO2, He, and SF6, in microgravity can lead to the development of more efficient and less harmful fire suppression systems, reducing the risk of toxic byproducts during fire events.

literature.title: FLEX: A Decisive Step Forward in NASA's Combustion Research Program
literature.link_rule: 'FLEX' + combustion term in title/abstract
literature.abstract: Stemming from the need to prevent, detect and suppress on-board spacecraft fires, the NASA microgravity combustion research program has grown to include fundamental research. From early experiment, we have known that flames behave differently in microgravity, and this environment would provide an ideal laboratory for refining many of the long held principals of combustion science. A microgravity environment can provide direct observation of phenomena that cannot be observed on Earth. Through the years, from precursor work performed in drop towers leading to experiments on the International Space Station (ISS), discoveries have been made about the nature of combustion in low gravity environments. These discoveries have uncovered new phenomena and shed a light on many of the fundamental phenomena that drive combustion processes. This paper discusses the NASA microgravity combustion research program taking place in the ISS Combustion Integrated Rack, its various current and planned experiments, and the early results from the Flame Extinguishment (FLEX) Experiment.

literature.title: Methanol Droplet Combustion in Oxygen-Inert Environments in Microgravity
literature.link_rule: 'FLEX' + combustion term in title/abstract
literature.abstract: The Flame Extinguishment (FLEX) experiment that is currently underway in the Combustion Integrated Rack facility onboard the International Space Station is aimed at understanding the effects of inert diluents on the flammability of condensed phase fuels. To this end, droplets of various fuels, including alkanes and alcohols, are burned in a quiescent microgravity environment with varying amounts of oxygen and inert diluents to determine the limiting oxygen index (LOI) for these fuels. In this study we report experimental observations of methanol droplets burning in oxygen-nitrogen-carbon dioxide and oxygen-nitrogen-helium gas mixtures at 0.7 and 1 atmospheric pressures. The initial droplet size varied between approximately 1.5 mm and 4 mm to capture both diffusive extinction brought about by insufficient residence time at the flame and radiative extinction caused by excessive heat loss from the flame zone. The ambient oxygen concentration varied from a high value of 30% by volume to as low as 12%, approaching the limiting oxygen index for the fuel. The inert dilution by carbon dioxide and helium varied over a range of 0% to 70% by volume. In these experiments, both freely floated and tethered droplets were ignited using symmetrically opposed hot-wire igniters and the burning histories were recorded onboard using digital cameras, downlinked later to the ground for analysis. The digital images yielded droplet and flame diameters as functions of time and subsequently droplet burning rate, flame standoff ratio, and initial and extinction droplet diameters. Simplified theoretical models correlate the measured burning rate constant and the flame standoff ratio reasonably well. An activation energy asymptotic theory accounting for time-dependent water dissolution or evaporation from the droplet is shown to predict the measured diffusive extinction conditions well. The experiments also show that the limiting oxygen index for methanol in these diluent gases is around 12% to 13% oxygen by volume.

literature.title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

literature.abstract: The Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) program is a continuing set of experiments on droplet combustion, performed employing the Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA), inside the chamber of the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), which is located in the Destiny module of the International Space Station (ISS). This report describes the experimental hardware, the diagnostic equipment, the experimental procedures, and the methods of data analysis for FLEX. It also presents the results of the first 284 tests performed. The intent is not to interpret the experimental results but rather to make them available to the entire scientific community for possible future interpretations.

title.value: Gradient Driven Fluctuation Experiment

objectives.value:
The primary objectives of the GRADFLEX investigation can be summarized as follows:

To investigate non-equilibrium fluctuations in microgravity by studying the behavior of gradient-driven fluctuations in a microgravity environment, where the stabilizing influence of gravity is significantly reduced.

To measure the divergence of large-size fluctuations by observing and quantifying this divergence up to the limits imposed by the sample size.

To quantify the amplitude and spatial extent of fluctuations by precisely measuring the mean-squared amplitude of the fluctuations as a function of both wave vector (spatial extent) and frequency (temporal dynamics).

 The investigation aims to rigorously test existing theoretical models of non-equilibrium fluctuations including comparing the measured amplitude and q-dependence of S(q) with predictions, both on Earth and in microgravity.

Beyond the static properties (amplitude and spatial extent), the investigation also seeks to characterize the temporal dynamics of the fluctuations.

approach.value: The GRADFLEX experiment investigated gradient-driven fluctuations in fluids using a dual approach: a 12-day microgravity flight experiment aboard the Foton-M3 satellite and complementary ground-based tests with the same apparatus. Two fluid systems (CS₂ and polystyrene/toluene) were subjected to precisely controlled temperature gradients. Quantitative shadowgraphy, a sensitive optical technique, measured both static (S(q)) and dynamic (S(q,ω)) properties of the fluctuations, with images acquired at specific rates for each. Data analysis involved Fourier transforms and spectral techniques to extract fluctuation amplitudes and dynamics and to address unexpected noise. The core of the study was a rigorous, parameter-free comparison of experimental results with theoretical predictions for both terrestrial and microgravity environments. The approach combined and refined a sophisticated design, enabling robust testing.

hypothesis.value: In the absence of gravity, thermally-driven fluctuations in a fluid subjected to a temperature gradient will exhibit significantly enhanced amplitude and spatial extent, with their mean-squared amplitude diverging with the size of the fluctuation and exhibiting altered dynamics up to the limits imposed by the sample dimensions.

research_impacts.value: Throughout the course of this work it has been necessary to constantly improve the experimental method of choice, namely the quantitative shadowgraph. This development has now reached the stage where it is clear that this method, if handled properly, represents a viable method of carrying out both dynamic and static light scattering at scattering angles so small as to defy the imagination of of anyone who has worked in the field. Although it is likely to take some time for the knowledge we have gained to be disseminated, there is no reason this method cannot be added to the scattering arsenal. Furthermore, it can also be applied to X-rays, enabling one to extend the lower limit of X-ray scattering as well. The consequences of putting a new technique into the hands of researchers is difficult to asses in advance. Basically, however, this method will enable quantitative measurements of various systems having size ranges that are too large for existing techniques. Obvious examples are the crystallization process in colloidal systems, gelation processes, and aggregation and flocculation. Because scattering provides excellent statistical averages, the method should prove quite complementary to visualization techniques such as microscopy.

microgravity.sentence: To investigate non-equilibrium fluctuations in microgravity by studying the behavior of gradient-driven fluctuations in a microgravity environment, where the stabilizing influence of gravity is significantly reduced.

The investigation aims to rigorously test existing theoretical models of non-equilibrium fluctuations including comparing the measured amplitude and q-dependence of S(q) with predictions, both on Earth and in microgravity.

The GRADFLEX experiment investigated gradient-driven fluctuations in fluids using a dual approach: a 12-day microgravity flight experiment aboard the Foton-M3 satellite and complementary ground-based tests with the same apparatus.
The core of the study was a rigorous, parameter-free comparison of experimental results with theoretical predictions for both terrestrial and microgravity environments.

title.value: Isothermal Dendritic Growth Experiment - Second United States Microgravity Payload - 2

objectives.value: The primary objective of the microgravity dendritic growth experiment was to measure definitively the kinetics and morphology of dendritic growth, and to account for the effects of natural convection. The experimental objective was to use a single,clearly defined experimental parameter, namely, the supercooling, to fully determine the resulting steady-state dendritic growth velocity, V, and tip radius R. Designated the IDGE, the first flight, manifested on the second United States Microgravity Payload (USMP-2) mission, was launched and operated on the STS-62 on March 4-18, 1994. This IDGE investigation met the objective of acquiring accurate dendritic growth speed and morphology data under diffusion-controlled conditions, while greatly reducing buoyancy-induced convective heat transport through the reduction of gravity. The microgravity environment broadened this range of supercooling and permitted for the first time a critical assessment of both the heat transport theory and the interfacial kinetics behavior.

approach.value:
The approach was to observe and image dendritic growth as a function of undercooling such that dendritic tip velocities and radii could both be accurately measured and used as a critical test of theory. Succinonitrile (SCN), transparent when molten, was used as a model metal analog system for studying dendritic growth since it solidifies like the body centered cubic (BCC) ferrous metal alloys, i.e., with an atomically ''rough'' solid-liquid interface. In addition, SCN displays convenient properties for solidification experiments, such as a low melting temperature (58.08 °C), optical transparency, and the potential for accurate characterization of its thermophysical properties. Dendritic growth is initiated inside the experimental chamber by energizing thermoelectric coolers attached to one end a thin capillary injector tube called the stinger. The other end of the stinger, where the dendrite emerges in the center of the chamber, is notched, much like the tip of a fountain pen. This helps isolate the leading dendrite and reduces the time needed until the leading dendrite is isothermal and has achieved steady state.
The IDGE flight experiment was divided into 60 operational cycles. The first cycle, the warm-up cycle, consists of bringing the system up to the operational temperature where all system components are checked and initialized. The second cycle measured the liquidus temperature of the SCN as a calibration point from which all subsequent supercoolings are measured. The remaining cycles were dendritic growth cycles where dendrites are grown and photographed at varying supercoolings. For each dendritic growth cycle, the experiment obtained a time series of stereo-pairs of 35-mm photographic images, low-resolution, binary, digitized electronic images and various data streams characterizing the dendrite's growth conditions during the cycle. For each image pair, either 35-mm film negative or digitized image, we measured the position of the dendrite tip, and the associated time that the image was recorded. The dendritic velocity was determined by calculating the slope of the displacement-time curve from the steady-state regime of the growth cycle. The velocity is then adjusted by appropriate stereographic and magnification factors. This procedure yields a set of dendrite velocity measurements accurate to about ± 2 percent.

hypothesis.value: The hypothesis of this investigation is that as a function of the supercooling there exists an explicit dendritic dynamic operating state defined by dendritic tip velocity, V and the dendrite tip paraboloidal radius of curvature, R. The Peclet number obtained from the Ivantsov solution for each specified supercooling yielded an infinite number of solutions for V and R. Therefore it is hypothesized that a second independent equation or length scale exists, which, when combined with the Ivantsov diffusion solution, will mathematically select the observed unique dynamic operating state. Two of the candidates for the additional crystal growth physics that could provide the second  crucial equation are the effects from the solid-melt interfacial energy, the influence of temperature fluctuations in  the melt, or both.

research_impacts.value: The size, shape, spacing, and orientation of the dendrites in cast metal alloys have a major effect on the strength, ductility and toughness. Nearly all cast-metal alloys used in everyday products, such as automobiles and airplanes, are composed of dendritic microstructures. Metallurgists have long sought to predict and control alloy microstructures. The development of automated, cost effective manufacturing techniques ultimately depends on the precision with which the problem in non-equilibrium pattern formation can be solved. In principle, the intent is to incorporate fundamental understanding of microstructures into computer codes that simultaneously help  design materials with made to order properties and optimize their manufacturability and performance. Dendritic growth experiments conducted in the microgravity environment can provide benchmark data to validate such predictive models.

title.value: Isothermal Dendritic Growth Experiment United States Microgravity Payload-3

objectives.value: Following the first IDGE flight on USMP-2, the second fight of lDGE took place on USMP-3 in February and March of 1996. The scientific objectives of the second flight of the IDGE was to: characterize the three-dimensional shape of a dendrite tip; accumulate a dense data set on dendritic velocities and radii in the diffusion-limited infinite boundary regime; and to form dendritic velocity data sets to clarify issues in the literature about whether convection or near-field boundary conditions affect the dendritic growth measurements in microgravity in the lower supercooling range.

approach.value: The sample material and temperature controls were identical to the USMP-2 investigation. In addition to the high-resolution film data collected after the shuttle landed, growth velocities were measured in near-real time by downlinked, binary CCD images. Many growths were measured from CCD images alone and these steady-state velocity measurements were accurate to 2%.

hypothesis.value: The hypothesis of this investigation is that as a function of the supercooling there exists an explicit dendritic dynamic operating state defined by dendritic tip velocity, V and the dendrite tip paraboloidal radius of curvature, R. The Peclet number obtained from the Ivantsov solution for each specified supercooling yielded an infinite number of solutions for V and R. Therefore it is hypothesized that a second independent equation or length scale exists, which, when combined with the Ivantsov diffusion solution, will mathematically select the observed unique dynamic operating state. Two of the candidates for the additional crystal growth physics that could provide the second  crucial equation are the effects from the solid-melt interfacial energy, the influence of temperature fluctuations in  the melt, or both. Aside from the original hypothesis for USMP-2, the USMP-3 also tested the hypothesis that both the magnitude of the microgravity level and the growth angle with respect to the quasi-static microgravity vector would affect the growth velocity. With additional and sufficient data from USMP-3 it was anticipated to construct a three-dimensional reconstruction of the non-parabolic, non-body-of-revolution dendritic tip shape.

title.value: Isothermal Dendritic Growth Experiment United States Microgravity Payload - 4

objectives.value: Following the first and second IDGE flight on USMP-2 and USMP-3, the third and final IDGE flight (USMP-4) was launched on STS-87, in November of 1997. The last flight employed  pivalic acid (PVA)—a face centered cubic (FCC) organic plastic crystal that solidifies analogous to many non–ferrous metals unlike SCN that solidifies similar to BCC ferrous metal alloys. In comparison to SCN, PVA exhibits a large anisotropy of its solid–melt interfacial energy. The primary objective was to investigate if the anisotropy of solid-melt interfacial energy is indeed a key physical parameter in the subtle selection process of dendritic operating states.

approach.value: The experimental approach was similar to USMP-3 and USMP-4 with the exception that PVA was utilized as the sample material to quantify growth velocity as a function of undercooling. In addition, the spacing between nearest neighbors were also quantified during this USMP-4 investigation.

hypothesis.value: The hypothesis of the IDGE investigations is that as a function of the supercooling there exists an explicit dendritic dynamic operating state defined by dendritic tip velocity, V and the dendrite tip paraboloidal radius of curvature, R. The Peclet number obtained from the Ivantsov solution for each specified supercooling yielded an infinite number of solutions for V and R. Therefore it is hypothesized that a second independent equation or length scale exists, which, when combined with the Ivantsov diffusion solution, will mathematically select the observed unique dynamic operating state. Two of the candidates for the additional crystal growth physics that could provide the second  crucial equation are the effects from the solid-melt interfacial energy, the influence of temperature fluctuations in  the melt, or both. Aside from the original hypothesis for USMP-2, the USMP-3 also tested the hypothesis that both the magnitude of the microgravity level and the growth angle with respect to the quasi-static microgravity vector would affect the growth velocity. With additional and sufficient data from USMP-3 it was anticipated to construct a three-dimensional reconstruction of the non-parabolic, non-body-of-revolution dendritic tip shape. For the final USMP-4 investigation the use PVA was to test the hypothesis if interfacial anisotropy has any significant effect on growth velocity and if there exist a minimum nearest neighbor distance below which the growth velocity begins to decrease due to overlapping of thermal fields.
