title.value: Solidification Using a Baffle in Sealed Ampoules

objectives.value: There are both technology demonstration objectives and scientific objectives. The technology demonstration objectives are to test the performance of an automatically moving baffle in microgravity and to determine the behavior and possible advantages of liquid encapsulation in microgravity conditions.The science objectives are to visualize the melt/encapsulant behavior in microgravity and to grow doped InSb without dewetting. The key goal of SUBSA was to clarify the origin of the melt convection in space and to reduce the magnitude to the point that it does not interfere with the transport phenomena.

approach.value: In the space environment, accelerations produce circular motions that affect the solidification of crystal growth/semiconductor materials flight experiments, resulting in a material that is less useful.The objectives of SUBSA are:Test the performance of an automatically moving baffle (used to minimize melt motion).Visualization of the melting process to identify what causes the melt motion.Production of several crystals with reproducible properties.To determine the behavior and possible advantages of liquid encapsulation in microgravity conditions.

hypothesis.value: A baffle placed inside a melt reduces the effective size of the melt and leads to a decrease in the amount of convection. The combined effect of microgravity (reduction of gravitational acceleration by a factor of 10^6 ) and a small zone melt (reduction of the size and temperature differential by a factor of 10^3 ) will generate the effective conditions of “nano-gravity” (the Rayleigh number will be reduced by a factor of 10^9 ).

research_impacts.value: The SUBSA furnace, with its capability to control and visualize melting and solidification of semiconductor crystals has increased our understanding of semiconductor crystal growth phenomena. The transparent furnace coupled with the video downlink and real-time commanding capability provided a powerful tool for scientists to watch the motion of the crystal-melt interface as semiconductor crystals were formed. The design of the SUBSA ampoule which includes a baffle and a system that prevents de-wetting resulted in crystals whose properties have not been disrupted by micro-accelerations at the Station, making it possible for future researchers to produce the high-quality semiconductor crystals that are in demand on Earth.

title.value: Tiegelfreies Elektromagnetisches Prozessieren Unter Schwerelosigkeit; Electromagnetic Processing

objectives.value:
The TEMPUS (Tiegelfreies ElektroMagnetisches Prozessieren Unter Schwerelosgkeit) facility is a research instrument designed to perform electromagnetic levitation studies in reduced gravity. TEMPUS was a joint undertaking between DARA, the German space agency, and the Microgravity Science and Applications Division of NASA. Specific objectives for the different investigations carried out by US Principal Investigators using this facility is categorized by different classes:
Class A: Studies of undercooling phenomena and the kinetics of nucleation (Prof. M. Flemings, MIT, Prof. R. Bayuzick, Vanderbilt Univ), Class B: Measurement of specific heat in liquid metals using an AC calorimetry technique (Prof W. Johnson, CALTECH), Class C: Measurement of viscosity and surface tension of undercooled metals (Prof. J. Szkeley, Prof. M. Flemings, MIT), Class D: Measurement of thermal expansion in undercooled materials (Prof W. Johnson, CALTECH).
In addition to the US Principal Investigators, available data from European investigations performed on TEMPUS and captured here include Viscosity and Surface Tension of Undercooled Metallic Melts (Dr. Egry, DLR, Germany), Thermophysical Properties of Undercooled Metallic Melts (Dr. Egry, DLR, Germany), Thermal Expansion of Glass forming Metallic Alloys in the Undercooled State (Dr. Samwer, Georg-August-Universitat Gottingen, Germany), and Thermodynamics and Glass Formation Undercooled Liquid Alloys (Dr. Wunderlich and Dr. Fecht, University of Ulm, Germany).

approach.value: Metallic samples of 7 or 8 mm diameter are positioned in the TEMPUS coils by electromagnetic forces and melted by induced currents. A ''squeezing'' force is then applied to a stably positioned liquid sample to induce oscillations. The rate of decay of the amplitude of these oscillations can be observed in order to measure the viscosity at different temperatures, while the frequency of the oscillation modes is used to deduce the surface tension at these temperatures. Measurements are planned on reactive, refractory melts (Zr), high-viscosity eutectics (ZrNi, PdSi), and industrial alloys (Fe-Cr-Ni) in addition to standard materials for comparison (Au, Ni). In addition, mathematical modeling designed to give a detailed understanding of what can be expected from prevailing conditions in the flight experiments was also developed.

hypothesis.value: Levitation, positioning and processing of materials which are not in direct contact with container surfaces, provides a unique opportunity to study a number of phenomena. In particular, the lack of contact with container walls reduces the possibility for heterogeneous nucleation in studies of the processing of molten materials. The study of the properties and solidification of undercooled materials is facilitated by containerless processing.

research_impacts.value: The accurate determination of the thermophysical properties of liquid materials is important for fundamental and practical reasons, including verification of atomistic models of the liquid state, nucleation studies of phase transition, and modeling of materials processing operations. In addition, these studies often focus on advanced materials such as metallic glass forming materials. Metallic glasses are an industrially important new class of materials. They are ductile, isotropic and corrosion resistant and are used in magnetic storage media films.

title.value: Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity

objectives.value: The objective of this investigation was to use numerical simulation to explore the influence of gravity on pyrolysis smoke growth from a fundamental perspective. The intention of this effort is to quantify the differences between microgravity and Earth gravity smoke, and to identify the fluid dynamic mechanisms that cause the differences.

approach.value: The formation and growth of dibutyl-phthalate (DBP) particles in Earth gravity and microgravity environments was simulated. Direct numerical simulation via a Navier-Stokes nodal approach was utlilized. The smoke originates from pyrolysis vapor expelled from a heated sample in a geometry similar to that considered in the SAME experiments. This study considered two cross-flow velocities of sufficiently low speed that buoyancy cannot be neglected in the presence of gravity. Simulations are presented to assess the dependence of particle size distributions on thermophoresis, particle settling, and flow geometry. The final report for this investigation introduces the simulation and modeling methodology, followed by a description of the flow geometry and the parameter space under consideration.The differences in the wake geometry attributable to buoyancy for the lower of two flow speeds was examined.  Instantaneous scalar fields were used to describe particle accumulation and growth in the buoyant and non-buoyant wakes that form downstream of the hot vapor source.

hypothesis.value: Without buoyancy, mixing and heat transfer are reduced, the time-temperature history of the combustion vapors (or particle precursors) and particle trajectories are significantly altered, changing the composition of the smoke. The chemical composition of the burning material also affects the characteristics of the smoke generated.

research_impacts.value: Models and tools that characterize particles generated as smoke can be used to ascertain how temperature, gravity, and material properties affect the smoke produced. This would directly lead to better smoke detection devices and prevent fires that can lead to loss of materiel and loss of life.

title.value: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

objectives.value: The objective of this ground investigation was to use flight data obtained from PSI through NASA’s Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) to quantify how externally imposed thermal and convective perturbations regulated the dynamics and ultimate fate of already established droplet cool flames, and to explain run-to-run variability by isolating the roles of deliberate heating and unintentional drift-induced convection. Focusing on both small and large droplets, the work mapped stability windows for ignition, sustained oscillation, transitions to hot ignition and warm-flame behavior, and extinction under microgravity. By leveraging and extending the FLEX data in the PSI, this study produced reusable models and sensitivity analyses that coupled low-temperature chemistry with transport and radiative effects.

approach.value:
OpenFOAM was used to develop a 3-D CFD model of n-alkane droplet cool flames in microgravity, coupling variable-density Navier–Stokes flow with low-temperature combustion chemistry, coupled heat and mass transfer, and radiation. Model fidelity was established against ISS FLEX measurements, after which controlled simulations examined three forcing modes (i) convection alone to mimic droplet drift, (ii) imposed heat flux, and (iii) combined convection plus heating applied to both large (1–4 mm) and sub-millimeter (~0.5 mm) droplets.

To accelerate progress, the study began with simplified chemistry and transitioned to reduced mechanisms for parameter sweeps over forcing amplitude and frequency, ambient composition (including ozone-assisted cases), and pressure. From each case, predictive observables were extracted (ignition delay, oscillation frequency and amplitude, stand-off and extinction diameters), and were used to construct stability maps that delineated conditions for cool-flame onset, persistence, and quenching. These maps were reconciled with FLEX observations and were used to guide next-generation test matrices for both large- and small-droplet experiments.

hypothesis.value: External thermo-convective perturbations (imposed temperature gradients, non-uniform heating, oscillatory/shear inflow) were expected to govern cool-flame ignition, oscillation, transition to hot ignition, and extinction by shifting residence time and scalar dissipation. In microgravity, where buoyancy was suppressed, this forcing was anticipated to dominate transport. A multidimensional, multi-physics CFD model was used to map perturbation-dependent stability boundaries and predict observables for comparison with FLEX data.

Space Benefits: Potential to improve spacecraft fire-safety modeling by resolving cool-flame/extinction behavior in microgravity; leverages FLEX to define safer operating envelopes/materials.
Earth Benefits: Advances low-temperature combustion understanding relevant to engine knock, efficiency, and emissions; delivers validated CFD tools transferrable to practical combustors.

title.value: Enhanced Particle Tracking in STDC Data and Its Industrial Application of Marangoni Convection

objectives.value: The primary objective this grant was to extract and understand the detailed thermo-fluid mechanics of the original NASA Surface Tension Driven Convection Experiment (STDCE-1) performed in microgravity, using modern diagnostic and computational tools. The study aims to revitalize the original video data found in PSI by applying advanced Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV) and Particle Tracking Velocimetry (PTV) methods, which provide higher resolution, sub-pixel accuracy, and robust flow field extraction compared to the limited analyses available in the early 1990s. By systematically comparing velocity and pressure fields obtained from these reanalyzed datasets with theoretical perturbation methods and COMSOL Multiphysics computational models, the project seeks to isolate the fundamental role of Marangoni convection and interfacial curvature in driving oscillatory and steady-state flows. Complementary ground-based experiments incorporating gravitational effects will be conducted to disentangle the relative contributions of buoyancy and surface tension-driven convection. These objectives ultimately support both NASA’s PSI solicitation  by expanding the scientific return from legacy datasets and advancing applied understanding for industrial processes that rely on controlled Marangoni flows, such as wafer drying, thin-film coating, and microfluidic device operation.

approach.value: The approach combined archival microgravity data analysis, computational modeling, and ground experiments to study surface tension driven convection (STDC). Video data from the original NASA STDCE-1 experiments were re-analyzed using several modern particle tracking techniques, including four MATLAB-based codes, three ImageJ-based codes, and sub-pixel localization methods, to produce velocity and pressure fields. These flow fields were compared with theoretical models derived from perturbation methods and with computational simulations performed in COMSOL Multiphysics® v5.6 that incorporated boundary conditions and curved free-surface geometries. In parallel, ground-based STDC experiments were carried out to examine gravitational effects and to distinguish buoyancy-driven flows from thermocapillary convection. This combination of data reanalysis, numerical simulation, and experimental testing provided a means to identify the influence of interfacial curvature, surface stresses, and geometry on Marangoni convection.

hypothesis.value: Re-analyzing NASA’s STDCE-1 microgravity video data with advanced particle tracking and computational modeling to reveal previously inaccessible details of thermo-fluid mechanics in surface tension driven convection. These insights, validated against ground-based experiments, aimed to clarify the interplay between Marangoni forces, interfacial curvature, and flow instabilities, leading to improved predictive models of thermocapillary flows.

research_impacts.value:
Space Benefits: Improves understanding of thermocapillary convection in microgravity, critical for designing reliable thermal management and materials processing systems aboard spacecraft. Provides validated numerical and theoretical models that can guide future ISS and space-based fluid physics experiments, reducing uncertainty from prior low-resolution analyses.
Earth Benefits: Supports industrial applications such as semiconductor wafer cleaning, thin-film coatings, welding, and liquid crystal display fabrication. Findings also translate to emerging fields like active matter and micro/nano robotics, where Marangoni flows and surface interactions could be harnessed for medical diagnostics, targeted drug delivery, and microplastics removal.

title.value: Light Microscopy Module Biophysics-2,5

objectives.value:
The primary objective of this investigation was to understand why protein crystallization experiments in microgravity have generated unexpectedly low or high numbers of crystals. Each outcome may cause experiments designed to obtain a small number of well-separated crystals to fail.

The objective of the proposed investigations is to explore the effects of a hitherto unstudied factor for the nucleation of protein crystals: solution shear flow. Besides providing a novel tool for nucleation control for protein crystallization experiments, the correlation between solution flows and protein crystal nucleation, to be tested in the proposed investigation, will shed light on one of the major mysteries of current space biophysics: the finding that in many cases the number of crystals nucleated in microgravity was greater or smaller than those nucleated on earth.

approach.value: Three cassettes containing five capillaries each were loaded with one of three proteins; (1) Lysozyme, (2) p53, and (3) hnRNPA-LC. The observation of these protein clusters were observed with a newly developed technique, called differential dynamic microscopy (DDM). DDM improves a recent method used to study and quantify the dynamics of sub-micrometer particles in solutions from fluctuations in intensity in optical micrographs. All samples were frozen to a temperature of -80C before flight to the ISS. The proteins were thawed and observed over several weeks in the ISS LMM module where they were filmed and photographed. Sample details and experimental parameters are summarized in LMMBio2_Experimental Table in the science document section.

hypothesis.value:
Hypothesis: The behavior of dense liquid clusters at different rates of convection will have a profound effect on crystal growth.

The main hypothesis underlying the proposed investigations consists of two parts:
1. The existence of nucleation precursors and the correlation between their properties and the nucleation rate can be used to control protein crystal nucleation via solution flow.
2. Enhancement or suppression of nucleation via solution flow, i.e., independently of solution supersaturation, can be used to achieve higher perfection of the grown crystals.
3. A very small fraction of the protein exists in a dense liquid phase in the form of Brownian particles, each a cluster of roughly 105 protein molecules undergoing liquid-like dynamics.
4. Crystal nucleation occurs when a small, ordered domain forms within the highly concentrated liquid-state environment of one of these particles.

research_impacts.value: These images provide data that help scientists and engineers understand the forces that control organization and dynamics of matter at microscopic scales. The organization and movement of matter on the microscopic level profoundly affects the macroscopic world and understanding such processes contributes to development of more efficient materials and machines for application on Earth.

title.value: Phase Transitions in Colloid-Polymer Mixtures in Microgravity

objectives.value: The objective of this PSI grant was to advance the understanding of phase transitions in colloid–polymer mixtures under microgravity conditions by integrating experimental observations with predictive modeling. Specifically, the research sought to determine how depletion interactions, arising from non-adsorbing polymers, influence the kinetics and morphology of phase separation and crystallization in complex fluids. By analyzing image data from NASA’s Binary Colloidal Alloy Test (BCAT-3 through BCAT-6) experiments conducted on the International Space Station, the project aimed to isolate the effects of gravity on phase behavior, quantify domain growth over multiple orders of magnitude in time and length scale, and develop a theoretical framework that connects these dynamics to hydrodynamic and thermodynamic parameters. Ultimately, this work sought to establish colloidal systems as model analogues for atomic and molecular phase transitions, providing insight relevant to both fundamental soft-matter physics and applied materials design.

approach.value: The approach combined data-driven analysis of PSI-archived BCAT imagery with a phase-field modeling framework that coupled the Cahn–Hilliard and Stokes equations to simulate phase separation in colloid–polymer mixtures. Experimental image sequences were processed for BCAT-3, -4 and -5, using algorithms in ImageJ and MATLAB to remove background noise, enhance contrast, and compute spatial autocorrelation functions for extracting characteristic domain length scales. Theoretical modeling of BCAT-5 incorporated concentration-dependent mobility and viscosity, along with Korteweg stresses to represent interfacial tension effects, allowing for the inclusion of hydrodynamic interactions that influenced domain coarsening. The governing equations were solved using a pseudospectral semi-implicit numerical scheme, and simulation results were quantitatively compared to flight data from the BCAT experiments. Model parameters were tuned using physical data from PSI to validate predictions and refine understanding of hydrodynamic coupling, phase-domain morphology, and kinetic arrest in colloid–polymer systems. This integrated experimental–theoretical approach yielded a comprehensive, microgravity-validated description of soft-matter phase transformation mechanisms.

hypothesis.value: Introducing non-adsorbing polymers into colloidal suspensions generates depletion-induced attractions that alter phase-transition kinetics; in microgravity, free from sedimentation and convection, these interactions can be directly modeled to reveal the intrinsic role of hydrodynamics in phase separation.

research_impacts.value: This research provided benchmark insight into soft-matter phase transitions without gravitational interference, improving predictive capability for self-assembly, crystallization, and gelation relevant to materials manufacturing and fluids research aboard the ISS. It has also improved understanding of phase-transition kinetics and rheology in colloid–polymer mixtures, informing materials science, pharmaceutical, and chemical engineering applications, and advancing the design of next-generation coatings, gels, and nanostructured materials.

title.value: Pool Boiling Heat Transfer Mechanisms in Low Gravity: Numerical Experiments of MABE and NPBX Data

objectives.value: The primary objectives for this PSI grant include establishing a deeper mechanistic understanding of nucleate boiling under low-gravity conditions by conducting high-fidelity numerical simulations that replicate the flight conditions of prior ISS-based boiling experiments, specifically MABE and NPBX. The investigation seeks to characterize key mechanisms governing bubble growth, waiting time, vapor spreading, coalescence, and detachment under variable gravity levels, degrees of wall superheat, and levels of liquid subcooling. Central to the objectives is quantifying how heat flux divides between nucleate boiling and natural convection modes, evaluating how the contact angle modulates wall adhesion forces, and determining the precise contribution of microlayer evaporation to heat transfer during low-gravity operation. By leveraging validated direct-numerical-simulation approaches tied to empirical MABE and NPBX measurements, this objective generates fundamental physics-based insights that enable predictive modeling of boiling processes relevant to spacecraft systems and advanced thermal architectures.

approach.value: The project approach was to use validated high-fidelity Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) ground-based computational simulations to numerically reproduce MABE- and NPBX-like boiling environments over a controlled range of heater temperatures, wall superheat conditions, and fluid subcooling levels. The research draws directly from ISS-acquired datasets that include detailed bubble growth dynamics, heat-flux profiles, and heater-surface imaging, which serve as reference benchmarks that guide simulation fidelity. Multiphase DNS simulations incorporate fluid phase-change physics, contact-line motion, interphase mass transport, and three-dimensional flow-field resolution to connect bubble behavior to instantaneous and time-averaged heat transfer. Iterative simulation campaigns then probe how variable gravitational acceleration, wettability contrast, bubble confinement, and microlayer evaporation influence overall heat-flux partitioning. The resulting database enables first-principles analysis of changes in boiling performance between terrestrial and microgravity settings while supporting quantitative model development applicable to spaceflight hardware, thermal architectures, and advanced electronic cooling systems.

hypothesis.value: The research was based on the hypothesis that, in microgravity, shifts in the relative influence of buoyancy, capillary forces, and microlayer evaporation fundamentally alter bubble-growth behavior and reduce heat-flux performance. It further hypothesized that these low-gravity effects can be accurately captured using high-fidelity Direct Numerical Simulations (DNS) validated against historic ISS boiling data from the MABE and NPBX experiments. By exploring variations in gravity, surface wettability, and thermal conditions, the study aimed to test the mechanisms governing bubble dynamics and heat transfer for application to spacecraft thermal management.

research_impacts.value:
Space Benefits: This investigation provides high-resolution insight into how boiling heat-transfer efficiency degrades under reduced gravity, enabling the development of more reliable spacecraft thermal-management systems that do not depend solely on buoyancy-driven vapor removal. Improved understanding of microlayer-based transport, contact-line wetting, spatial heat-flux distribution, and boiling-mode transition directly supports the design of future ISS and deep-space thermal architectures, power-electronics packaging, life-support thermal management, and compact, energy-efficient cooling platforms for extended-duration missions.


Earth Benefits: The computational foundations and physics-based insights gained through this study directly advance terrestrial thermal-management strategies for high-power electronic systems, including server-class processors, power-dense computing architectures, and high-performance energy-conversion systems. The work improves predictive control of boiling-induced heat removal, enabling higher operating throughput, greater component longevity, and reduced power consumption in heat-intensive commercial and defense electronics.

title.value: Quantitative Studies of Cool Flame Transitions at Radiation / Stretch Extinction Using Counterflow Flames

objectives.value:
By using the Flame Extinguishment (FLEX) experimental data from the Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) system of combustion science, the purpose of this grant was to conduct new simulations and ground-based experiments using ozone-sensitized counterflow flames to:
    1) Develop a new diagram of the flammability limits of diffusional cool flames affected by radiation, diffusion, and convection.
    2) Bridge the knowledge gap between the flammability limits and extinction limits of hot flames and cool flames.
    3) Verify the phenomena observed on the ISS flame extinguishment experiments.
    4) Obtain new, quantitative data of extinction limit, flame temperature, and species distribution for the validation of kinetic and radiation models involving cool flames.
    5) Extend the cool flame experiments from the original ISS droplet experiments to a more general ground-based combustion system involving radiation, diffusion, convection, and low-temperature chemistry while maintaining a one-dimensional geometry.

approach.value:
Using the experimental conditions of FLEX flight, a comparative studies of the oxygen concentration effects on the extinction limits of cool flames was conducted using three different numerical modeling schemes, (a) spark-assisted flame propagation of a n-heptane/air mixture, (b) one dimensional freely-propagating dimethyl ether (DME) flames using an arc-length continuation method and (c) simulated cool flame regimes and burning limits at elevated pressure (up to 20 atm) using DME/air mixtures.

Specific research details are outlined in the publication, ''Dynamics of cool flames'' [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pecs.2019.100787]; '' Understanding Cool Flames and Warm Flames'', [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.proci.2020.09.019] and ''Study of the low-temperature reactivity of large n-alkanes through cool diffusion flame extinction'', [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.combustflame.2017.01.028].

hypothesis.value: This investigation attempts to answer the critical question as to what conditions causes the hot flames transfer to cool flames and how the cool flame flammable region is related to hot flame flammability limit and extinction limit. The investigation hypothesizes that factors such as oxygen concentration, dilution, pressure, diffusion, and convection transport processes affect the cool flame transition.

research_impacts.value: Obtaining a fundamental understanding of the warm diffusion flame is particularly relevant to combustion in highly turbulent flow fields and in microgravity environments, owing to the possibility of long residence times. The results showed that the warm flame has a double reaction zone structure and plays a critical role in the transition between cool flames and hot flames. At elevated pressures, it was found that the flammable region of warm flames and cool flames expands due to the increase in low-temperature and intermediate-temperature reactivity with pressure. Since many real engines operate in the 20-40 atm pressure range, therefore, cool flames and warm flames are relevant and important flame regimes for high-pressure near-limit combustion applications. These calculations from this investigation will serve to advance the understanding of near-limit flame dynamics and provide guidance for experimental observation of different flame regimes.

title.value: Spurious Grain Formation in Alloys Directionally Solidified on the Space Station Due to Marangoni Convection

objectives.value: Develop a three dimensional solidification model incorporating Marangoni convection and thermosolutal convection which can predict formation of spurious grains during DS. Extract data, such as, fluid velocities along stream lines as a function of distance from the surface-void, angular rotation of the fragmented side arms due to Marangoni flow lines, etc. from PFMI (Pore Formation and Mobility Investigation) videos, and then compare these observations with the simulations in order to quantitatively validate our numerical model. Use that model to predict formation of spurious grains in a totally different alloy, Al-7Si (MICAST), under varying processing conditions, such as, during re-melting prior to DS, after a step increase or decrease in growth speed vs at constant speed, etc.

approach.value: Use the PFMI and MICAST experimental flight data available in PSI to validate a three dimensional solidification model to predict that formation of spurious grains during DS.

hypothesis.value:
Columnar and dendritic growth experiments in a predominantly diffusive microgravity environment have shown the presence of voids at the
melt-crucible interface which are the likely the source of Marangoni convective flows. It is hypothesized that it is this flow that is responsible for fragmentation of the dendrite-side arm, and its rotation which creates the nucleus for the subsequent growth and formation of spurious grains. This hypothesis was tested by numerically simulating the influence of the Marangoni convection on the trajectory of such a dendrite fragment in the alloy melt and comparing with the experimental observations.

title.value: Fabrication of Amorphous Metals in Space

objectives.value:
The primary objective of this investigation was to understand the effect of microgravity processing on composition and microstructure evolution in metallic glass forming alloys or bulk metallic glass (BMG). Specific questions to be answered were:

   (a) How does processing in microgravity change the composition of the matrix of the glass-forming alloys compared to processing in gravity?
   (b) How does the volume fraction of the W spheres affect the composition and properties of the matrix?
   (c) How does the composition and viscosity of the glass-forming alloy affect the diffusion of W in microgravity?
   (d) How do the different diameter of W spheres affect the diffusion of W into the matrix?
   (e) Does the dissolved W provide a mechanism to improve the wear resistance and toughness of the matrix by providing reinforcement for brittle phases?

approach.value: The objective of the flight experiment is to process 12 samples of two glass-forming alloys (Vitreloy 106 and Zr48Cu47.5Al4Co0.5) in microgravity with three different volume fractions of W spheres (5%, 15% and 30%) with two different diameters of W spheres (25-36 μm diameter and 140-150 μm diameter). The cast composite samples were 15 mm in diameter and 12 mm long cylinders. The W particles were distributed as homogeneously as possible without sedimentation. On orbit, the samples were loaded into the Low Gradient Furnace (LGF) on the Materials Science Research Rack. They were held for 120 minutes at 1,200 °C (1,473 K) in microgravity with the intent to dissolve the W particles into the matrix and to create a fine distribution of W dendrites homogenously distributed throughout. The samples were then  cooled back to room temperature slowly, solidifying the morphology and composition. The Vitreloy 106 samples were compared with Zr48Cu47.5Al4Co0.5 in terms of composition of the matrix, morphology of the W dendrites, and mechanical properties, with comparisons drawn between samples produced on-orbit and on the ground to distinguish the effects of microgravity.

hypothesis.value:
The hypothesis for the experiment is that microgravity promotes composite formation by stabilizing the interface between the W nano-particle nuclei and the bulk liquid. In contrast, on Earth, the heavy W particles would fall out of the system as they form. Therefore, the composition of the solid formed on Earth will differ from that formed in microgravity.

On Earth, the samples should solidify in a manner consistent with the Scheil solidification approximation meaning:
(a) liquid diffusion is instant over experimental timescales
(b) solid-state diffusion does not occur (solid falls out of the system as it forms)
(c) the solid composition profile will follow the solidus as the system cools, until all the liquid is consumed.

In contrast, in microgravity, the solid/liquid interface lifetime is much longer, so there is more opportunity for solid back-diffusion. For this case, the composition profile will approach (but not reach) that of the equilibrium solidification case. After processing in both gravity and microgravity, experimental compositional data at the matrix-sphere interface will be obtained. It is expected that composites formed on Earth will solidify consistent with Scheil solidification and composites formed in microgravity will deviate from Scheil, approaching equilibrium solidification.

research_impacts.value: The development of innovative new materials is a fundamental part of future terrestrial and space technologies. These materials have a tremendous benefit towards improving life on Earth, from improving the accessibility and cost of solar power, to making cars safer and stronger, to reducing the mass of aircraft, for example. Innovative technologies typically require new materials tailored for those applications. This drives materials development.

title.value: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases

objectives.value:
1. Plan and support flight testing on the International Space Station (ISS).
2. Determine the conditions for which cool diffusion flames occur for propane, n-butane, and n-pentane; normal and inverse flames; and a broad range of Zst, Tad, and fluent flow rate.
3. Support the flight tests with advanced CFD simulations.
4. Identify or develop a chemical kinetics mechanism that yields good agreement between the CFD predictions and the ISS measurements.
5. Disseminate the results as widely as possible.

approach.value: Perform spherical diffusion flame tests aboard the International Space Station. Consider multiple fuels, a range of reactant dilutions, flow rates, and pressures for normal and inverse convection directions. Observe the flames with a broad suite of cameras, radiometers, photomultiplier tubes, and thermocouples.

hypothesis.value:
The hypotheses of this research are that testing aboard the ISS can demonstrate the following for the first time, contributing to an improved understanding of cool flame kinetics.
  1. Steady-state cool diffusion flames on spherical porous burners.
  2. Cool diffusion flames burning propane, n-butane, and n-pentane.
  3. Cool diffusion flames for a wide range of Zst, Tad, and pressures.
  4. Inverse cool diffusion flames.
  5. Cool diffusion flames for which a decrease in fluent flow rate will cause extinction, whereas an increase will cause a transition to a hot diffusion flame, with oscillation possible between hot and cool flames.

research_impacts.value: Combustion provides 86% of the world’s energy and an even higher fraction of the energy used for transportation. The internal combustion engines used for transportation generally have thermal efficiencies of 38% or lower because of thermal losses. These efficiencies may increase to 60% if future engines can take advantage of ultra-lean combustion. However, this progress is being impeded by the limited understanding of the chemistry of cool flames. Research into cool diffusion flames (whose peak temperatures are 500 – 1000 K) has grown exponentially since they were discovered in 2012.  The measurements performed for this project will help to test and advance cool flame kinetics mechanisms. This should facilitate the development of more efficient internal combustion engines.

literature.abstract: From Nov. 2017 to Feb. 2022, the ACME project’s six independent investigations of laminar, non-premixed flames of gaseous fuels were conducted on the International Space Station (ISS) in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR).  An exploration of flames at the extremes of high sooting and high dilution was conducted with a coaxial coflow burner, where the fuel and oxidizer velocities were typically matched.  An investigation of electric-field effects also used the same coflow burner as well as a simple gas-jet burner, with a circular electrode mesh downstream of the burner, at voltages of either polarity up to 10 kV.  A study focused on material flammability in a quiescent atmosphere emulated the burning of condensed-phased fuels using cylindrical burners with a flat perforated outlet instrumented to measure the heat flux to the burner, i.e., emulated fuel.  Three studies of soot processes, flame dynamics, and low-temperature combustion used porous spherical burners yielding a nominally one-dimensional flame structure.  The ACME research will be represented through images and text.

While ISS testing has been completed for most of the studies in the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project, it is expected to continue into 2022.  The objectives and selected findings for each investigation are briefly discussed after a short review of the advantages of studying combustion in microgravity, previous research conducted in space, and the experimental hardware and its operation.

literature.title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) on the International Space Station (ISS)
literature.link_rule: 'Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments' + combustion term in title/abstract
literature.abstract: Experimental   studies   of   laminar,   non-premixed   flames   of   gaseous   fuels   are   underway   on   the International Space Station (ISS) as part of NASA’s Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments(ACME) project.  The research is primarily focused on improving practical terrestrial combustion through fundamental microgravity research, where a secondary objective is spacecraft fire safety.  Example goals are  to improve understanding of flame stability  and extinction limits, soot control and reduction, oxygen-enriched combustion which could enable practical carbon sequestration, combustion at fuel lean conditions where both optimum performance and low emissions can be achieved, the use of electric fields for combustion control, cool flame chemical kinetics, and materials flammability.  The microgravity environment avoids buoyancy-induced flicker and enables the creation of spherical flames, allowing numerical  models   to   focus   computational   power   on   transport   phenomena  and   chemical   kinetics. Compared to normal gravity, microgravity also provides longer residence times and larger length scales, yielding a broad range of flame conditions which are beneficial for simplified analysis, e.g., of limit behavior where chemical kinetics are important.  Using modular hardware, research for six independent investigations is being carried out within the station’s Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR).  While the ISS crew members set up the experimental hardware, the tests are remotely commanded with investigator input from the NASA Glenn Research Center.   Over a thousand flames have been ignited since ACME operations began in Sept. 2017 and selected results from the first five experiments are summarized.

literature.abstract: Thus far, studies of gaseous diffusion flames on the International Space Station (ISS) have been limited to research conducted in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) in mid-2009 and early 2012. The research was performed with limited instrumentation, but novel techniques allowed for the determination of the soot temperature and volume fraction. Development is now underway for the next experiments of this type. The Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project consists of five independent experiments that will be conducted with expanded instrumentation within the stations Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR). ACMEs goals are to improve our understanding of flame stability and extinction limits, soot control and reduction, oxygen-enriched combustion which could enable practical carbon sequestration, combustion at fuel lean conditions where both optimum performance and low emissions can be achieved, the use of electric fields for combustion control, and materials flammability. The microgravity environment provides longer residence times and larger length scales, yielding a broad range of flame conditions which are beneficial for simplified analysis, e.g., of limit behaviour where chemical kinetics are important. The detailed design of the modular ACME hardware, e.g., with exchangeable burners, is nearing completion, and it is expected that on-orbit testing will begin in 2016.

title.value: Ring-Sheared Drop - Interfacial Bioprocessing of Pharmaceuticals

objectives.value: The Ring-Sheared Drop (RSD) is a Microgravity Science Glovebox experiment that launched in July 2019 to the ISS to study shearing flow in the absence of solid walls. The major goals of this project were to adapt and use the RSD module to develop and test predictive models of non-Newtonian flow of high-concentration proteins at the interface.  Incorporating non-Newtonian constitutive equations for both interfacial and bulk flows and coupling the interfacial and bulk stresses is essential for mechanistic models that would be capable of predicting behavior under flow conditions of practical interest.  The coupled problem is intrinsically nonlinear and there is a need to develop robust and accurate numerical techniques to interrogate flow dynamics and experimentally validate and verify results.  The ring-sheared drop interfacial bioprocessing of pharmaceuticals-I (RSD-IBP-I) campaign aimed to study non-Newtonian interfacial hydrodynamics of the blood transport proteins bovine serum albumin (BSA) and human serum albumin (HSA) in microgravity.  Specifically, scientific aims focus on the effects of protein primary structure (BSA or HSA), protein concentration (4, 40, or 400 mg/mL), and interfacial shear rate (3, 10, or 30 rpm) on microgravity fluid flow, measured using velocimetry of hollow glass microsphere tracer particles within protein samples.  This campaign intended to confer improved understanding of interfacial protein flows in relation to physiology, the environment, and industry relevant to both spaceflight and Earth.

approach.value:
Preflight preparation included refurbishment of all test cells including modification of test cells S/N 101-106 to include the flight tested (both parabolic and ISS with the assistance of NASA MSFC) integrated deployment tube and upper ring design by TBE, refurbishment of all test cells used in the previous RSD-BPS campaign by TBE, preparation of protein samples and methodological ground controls.

Following sample installation, the RSD drop was deployed by extruding a drop from the deployment tube until pinning is achieved at the far ring.  Shearing was then commenced by rotation of the far ring, measurements recorded for startup, steady, and stop flows each at 3, 10, and 30 rpm.  Each 1.5 min. image sequence was then compressed to a portable video file and downlinked to the ground computer at RPI.  ISS flight campaigns occurred Summer 2022 and Spring 2023, achieving 92% of proposed science objectives with 121.5/132 sample videos successfully collected, meeting the criteria for complete success.  Additionally, 27 videos of interfacial aging and 24 micrographs of extra data were collected.  The RSD hardware concluded the campaign in a nominal configuration with good health and status after four years in space aboard the ISS.

Postflight: Test cells were returned June 30th 2023 on SpX-28 to TBE. Test cells appear to be in nominal pre-refurbishment configuration. RSD hardware remains in nominal configuration and good health.

hypothesis.value: The study of fluid interfaces coupled to bulk flows, including non-Newtonian response of either the interfacial or the bulk fluid can be uniquely advanced through experimentation in microgravity, where surface tension containment can be achieved at relatively large length scales.  If the hydrodynamics of concentrated protein solutions are precisely measured, then sufficiently descriptive viscosity constitutive relations can be selected or developed from fundamental physics to describe fluid behavior.

research_impacts.value: Coupled bulk and interfacial flow in the RSD, developed under this grant is currently being analyzed to aid in formulating a model of non-Newtonian interfacial hydrodynamics coupled to a Newtonian bulk flow. These results were recently submitted for publication in a special issue of the journal Fluids, entitled ''Non-Newtonian Flow: Interfacial and Bulk Phenomena.''  While all cases examined remain at least weakly coupled to the bulk flow, this investigation established the effective ranges of model parameters. Bulk flow profiles demonstrate moderate sensitivity of the bulk flow to the behavior of the air-liquid interface, in general increasing with higher Boussinesq number Bq (non-dimensionalized surface viscosity) while maintaining interface to bulk flow coupling. Furthermore, investigation of dissipation may be useful for gauging the interchange between the hydrodynamics and energetics of flow constituents. The change in Bq by the shear-thinning model is indicative of a change in structure of an constituent material. As such, changes in the shape of a constituent of a complex fluid induced by flow are reciprocal with the changes that manifest in flow behavior. Describing the stability of such reciprocal changes could lead to a better understanding of natural systems as well as improved control of transport phenomena.

title.value: Advanced Colloids Experiment -Temperature controlled- 2

objectives.value:
The objective of this experiment is the investigation of the assembly of complex structures from micron-scale colloidal particles interacting via tunable attractive interactions. Regulating temperature enables control of particle interactions.

This simple reversible process is controlled by adjusting the size of the tunable temperature fluctuations in a two-component fluid (solvent).  In principle, the ingredients are simple: particles suspended in a binary solvent, without the addition of any other components.

By studying this process based on critical Casimir forces in microgravity, where sedimentation and convection are essentially removed, we will learn how to adjust complex attractive particle interactions. This simple reversible process is controlled by adjusting the size of the tunable temperature fluctuations in a two-component fluid (solvent).  In principle, the ingredients are simple: particles suspended in a binary solvent, without the addition of any other components.

Understanding self-assembly processes like the critical Casimir effect will teach ways to grow complex nanostructured materials. Furthermore, these experiments will provide fundamental insight into the nature of temperature-controlled super structure assembly, the relation between complex interactions and complex equilibrium and non-equilibrium structures, and the dynamics of both equilibrium and non-equilibrium growth processes.

1- Short mix of sample.
2- Ramp temperature to find critical temperature and reduce temperature and initiate a very long mix of sample.

6- Mix sample followed by stepwise temperature ramp with image stacks.

title.value: Unified Support for THERMOLAB - ISS, ICOPROSOL and PARSEC

objectives.value:
Specific objectives of this investigation were as follows:
   • Plan and develop experiment parameter sets to investigate anomalous nucleation events in zirconium samples during ISS-EML experiments
   • Analyze cavitation-induced nucleation experiments on zirconium and zirconium-nickel alloys
   • Analyze fluid flow during ISS-EML experiments to support collaborators investigations
   • Continue flight preparations and development of experimental parameter sets for upcoming experiments in Batch 3
   • Provide magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) modeling support of macroconvection in various materials for three ESA sponsored projects: PARSEC, THERMOLAB - ISS, ICOPROSOL.

approach.value:
• The anomalous nucleation events of interest are hypothesized to be caused by cavitation in the melt. Experiments replicated the conditions in which the nucleation events were previously observed and explored similar experimental conditions.
• Magnetohydrodynamic modeling of fluid flow is to be used to determine the flow conditions during ISS-EML experiments. Relevant parameters include fluid velocity, shear rates, turbulence intensity, and their distribution. Such data is critical for control of experiments and input to other theoretical and modeling efforts.

hypothesis.value:
• Dynamic nucleation is an effect of the fluid flow and not reliant on classical nucleation theory.
• Thermophysical property measurements may require appropriate flow conditions, which should be quantified
• Flow conditions may affect solidification and nucleation behavior
• Oxygen may influence surface tension measurements in metallic melts

research_impacts.value:
Containerless processing provides access to the deeply undercooled region of metallic melts. Using this unique processing environement we are able to investigate fundamental solidification behaivor and meausure thermophysical properties of metallic melts including density, surface tension, viscosity, thermal expansion, heat capacity, thermal conductivity, and electrical conductivity. More specifically, impacts and benefits are broken out by the 3 associated flight experiments.

In PARSEC,  the effect of fluid flow on the solidification path of certain alloys is investigated. Control of the solidification path would enable tailoring of the microstructure and properties of metal parts for specific applications.

In ThermoLAB, the thermophysical properties of high-temperature materials is investigated. Many of these materials are used commercially. A better understanding of the physical properties will allow more efficient and more reliable production of metallic parts using these alloys. Other alloys are chosen because of scientific interest in their properties, which may illuminate fundamental physics related to the formation of bulk metallic glasses and quasicrystals.

The nucleation and growth of quasicrystals, and the effect of atomic-scale order on the macroscopic properties of these alloys is investigated in ICOPROSOL. This fundamental investigation may improve our ability to tailor the microstructure of metals for commercial applications.

title.value: Advanced Colloids Experiment - Imaging, Folding and Assembly of Colloidal Molecules

objectives.value: In ACE-T9, the imaging capability, folding dynamics, and assembly behavior of linear colloidal chains, colloidal dimers, and lock-and-key particles were studied by the combination of a proper design of particle architecture and tunable colloidal interactions (e.g., double layer repulsion and hydrophobic attraction). In the case of colloidal chains, for example, the single chain dynamics should sensitively depend on the chain flexibility and monomer-solvent interactions. Under the microgravity environment, we hoped to observe qualitative three-dimensional, real-time dynamics of single colloidal chains (using pre-confocal - bright field and fluorescent microscopy. We also aimed to observe three-dimensional structures assembled from colloidal dimers and lock-and-key particles and to measure the binding equilibrium constants that are impossible to measure in earth experiments due to the effect of sedimentation.

approach.value: The imaging goal is to observe (1) real-time and three-dimensional particle centroid positions of colloidal chains over both short (30 minutes) and long period (one week); (2) assembled structures, crystallites, and resolve particle centroid positions for colloidal dimers and Janus spheres. For short-time imaging, the video should be taken with 5 fps over 30 minutes. For both cases, the x-y positions of particles should be determined with less than 5% error (with respect to particle diameter). The z-positions should be determined within 1 micron. For fluorescence imaging, lamp should be shuttered between image sets to prevent sample bleaching.

hypothesis.value: In the microgravity environment, we will study the folding dynamics of single colloidal chains where the chain architecture can be varied systematically, and the monomer-solvent interaction can be tuned by varying salt concentrations. Furthermore, by tuning the balance between electric double layer repulsion and hydrophobic attraction on both colloidal dimers and lock-and-key particles, we aim to study the assembly of those colloidal molecules into complex three-dimensional structures and measure the binding equilibrium constants. This set of experiments provide insight into the relation between particle shape, colloidal interaction and structure. With the wide variety of attributes that characterize anisotropic interactions, we will probe previously inaccessible regions of complex phase space. Our studies will move significantly beyond hard spheres and towards experimental models appropriate for studying fundamental questions associated with complex symmetries.

research_impacts.value: In-situ manipulation of anisotropic interactions and dynamic pathways, based on rational colloidal particle design and proper use of external fields, could lead to crystalline and a periodic structures beyond those seen in nature. Results from this study will lead to improved control of non-covalent assembly of molecules, efficient tailoring of lattice symmetries, and the scalable processing of nano-structured materials. The development of new colloidal molecules and their associated assembled structures have considerable technological impact as well. Such structures will generally lead to arrays with reduced symmetry and enhanced directionality. They can interact with a broad range of electromagnetic radiation in unique ways and can exhibit collective photonic, plasmonic, mechanical, electronic, or magnetic properties that are not manifested at the level of single particles. As a result, they have significant potential as next-generation functional materials.

title.value: Advanced Colloids Experiment - Aging Dynamics and Stress-Relaxation in Colloidal Gels Studied in Microgravity

objectives.value:
Colloidal stability is critical to soft matter systems, especially to consumer products. These structures change in time, by processes know as coarsening - meaning the spacing between particles compact. This compaction continually changes this structure. When the structures created in the products can longer resist the gravitational stresses (e.g. buoyancy) on the structures, they collapse. The collapse, such as those that occur in geological formations during earthquakes, is often abrupt and without warning (delayed collapse). This is the essence of product instability. For some systems, the gel collapse can be anticipated by precursors, that can potentially be detected and forecasted.

This research will have significant impacts in two areas:
     •	It is not clear how the microscopic structure and its dynamics are related to the gel mechanical properties. The structure evolution controls the aging of the gel, and, on earth, this eventually leads to collapse. This work may significantly enhance the knowledge necessary to advance this important area of science.
     •	Second, relaxation of localized stresses in an amorphous solid brought by a rapid solidification process is ubiquitous in nature and can damage and destroy the materials. Besides affecting the rheological properties of the materials, these dynamics rule the aging of the thermal systems at rest. The detection of failure precursors, as the ones discovered in our colloidal gel, can potentially allow us to forecast the material failure before catastrophic rupture.

approach.value:
The ACE-T10 experiment exploited the Fluids Integrated Rack (FIR) and the Light Microscopy Module (LMM). The Light Microscopy Module (LMM) is an automated microscope. It permitted flexible imaging (e.g., bright field, dark field, phase contrast, confocal microscopy) for physics experiments and can be controlled remotely from the ground. The LMM accommodated sample change-out and fluid containment and included a glove box for on-orbit sample manipulation.

The ACE-T10 experiment used include confocal microscopy, which utilized a 532-nm frequency-doubled Nd:YAG laser, a confocal scanner, and an 8- to 12-bit digital CCD camera. The scanner captured 30 frames per second of confocal images by the CCD camera. A sample’s three-dimensional crystal structure can thus be reconstructed by assembling individual slices with an image analysis program. This information, in turn, enabled the observation and measurement of the colloidal growth, structure, and dynamics. The confocal module was attached and aligned to the side of the LMM. The microscope used a reflecting mirror to direct the light to and from the sample.

ACE-T10 utilized 6 capillary cells in 2 holding modules. The capillary cells, each contained about 20 microliters of the sample fluid and a magnetic stainless steel stir bar. Samples were stirred prior to example. The sample temperature was adjusted between 20 – 60 °C in order to find the transition temperature where the sample became a gel.

hypothesis.value: ACE-T10 delivered unique insights into the restructuring behavior of thermo-reversible colloidal gels, a topic of noticeable interest for the community of scientists dealing with soft materials. In normal gravity experiments, the ACE-T10 science team found evidence that the aging of these soft gels proceed via a sequence of sudden intermittent bursts of dynamical activity that resembles the ‘critical avalanche’ phenomena observed in several driven systems. The evidence collected suggests that, in a soft solid, these avalanches may be triggered by thermal agitation and occur spontaneously, even in the absence of other external forces. However, because of the density difference between the fluid and the particles in the gel network, gravity may play a role as well. Performing the ACE-T10 experiment in microgravity provided a unique opportunity to determine the gravity contribution.

research_impacts.value: Earth benefits/spin-off applications include understanding the behavior of weak gels and their aging can help materials scientists to make consumer product with longer shelf lives. In addition, because several features of the failure dynamics of disordered materials are system independent,  the results obtained using this model colloidal system can be generalized to other materials. This potentially can help to develop new way to characterize aging material and suggest their replacement before catastrophic failure.

title.value: Advanced Colloids Experiment-Nanoparticle Haloing

objectives.value:
Nanoparticle Haloing (NPH) is a colloidal stabilization technique that has been discovered relatively recently.  In NPH, highly charged nanoparticles are used to stabilize much larger (by 2 orders of magnitude or more), non-charged particles.  To accomplish this stabilization, the volume fraction of nanoparticles within the suspension need only be on the order of 1e-5 up to 1e-4 to stabilize at 1 to 2 vol% suspension of the larger particles.

The objective of this work is to gain fundamental insight into the physics of NPH with the aim of addressing the following unresolved questions:
   • How will NPH suspensions behave in thermal or electrical field gradients as they do under gravity?
   • How does the halo form or re-form if disturbed?
   • Can NPH (and manipulation thereof) be used to assemble and reconfigure colloidal crystals?
   • How does the nanoparticle charge impact halo formation?

approach.value:
The ACE-T12 experiment utilizes the Fluids Integrated Rack (FIR) and the Light Microscopy Module (LMM). The FIR is built to accommodate a wide range of experiments.

Accordingly, the ACE-T12 experiment included confocal microscopy, which used a 532-nm frequency-doubled Nd:YAG laser, a confocal scanner, and an 8- to 12-bit digital CCD camera on a Leica DM-RXA microscope. The scanner captured 30 frames per second of confocal images by the CCD camera.

ACE-T12 utilizes capillary cells. Three capillary cells with different concentrations of nanoparticles were provided in a sample module. Here is a brief high-level descriptive outline of the investigation on-orbit procedures that gives general experiment steps for each capillary.
1- Short mix of sample.
2- Ramp temperature to find critical temperature and reduce temperature and initiate a very long mix of sample.
3- Determine Region of Interest (ROI).
4- Ramp temperature continuously while imaging.
5- Mix sample followed by Single temperature step visits.
6- Mix sample followed by stepwise temperature ramp with image stacks.

hypothesis.value: When NPH suspensions were allowed to settle under gravity, those that were stabilized (while in suspension) formed highly ordered, 3-dimensional colloidal crystal structures. Current theory suggests that nanoparticles create a charge layer by forming a cage, or Halo, around the larger particles. Another hypothesis regarding the NPH stabilization mechanism focuses entirely on nanoparticle adsorption to the surface of the larger particle.  Based on the measurement of the interaction forces between two larger colloidal surfaces in a nanoparticle suspension, it was found that the force curves obtained could be fitted using a model based on nanoparticle adsorption.

research_impacts.value: Ultimately, the ability to design colloidal particles with a variety of well-controlled three-dimensional bonding symmetries opens a wide spectrum of new structures for colloidal self-assembly, beyond particle assemblies whose structures are defined primarily by repulsive interactions and shape. Such materials might include photonic crystals with programmed distributions of defects. Optical technology utilizing such materials may offer intriguing solutions to unavoidable heat generation and bandwidth limitations facing the computer industry.

title.value: Micromechanics Based Modeling of Cement Solidified in the Microgravity

objectives.value:
Micromechanics‑Based Modeling of Cement Solidified in the Microgravity aimed to advance knowledge of the mechanical properties of cement binders formed in reduced gravity by leveraging microgravity materials data, such as SEM/BSE micrographs, available in the PSI database.
This project sought to connect microstructure (e.g., porosity, phase morphology such as portlandite) observed in ISS‑cured tricalcium silicate (C3S) pastes to bulk mechanical/transport behavior through modeling, thereby informing design and engineering of cementitious materials for extraterrestrial construction and providing validated simulation data that scale sparse flight samples to application‑relevant sizes.

approach.value:
In this work, the micromechanics analysis code with generalized method of cells (MAC/GMC) was used to predict the structure-property relationship of these unique cement samples.
First, the sparse data of cement hydrated in microgravity environment was converted to high-fidelity 3D microstructure with the aid of a deep learning-based microstructure methodology. The reconstructed sub-volumes were compared against micro-CT data using statistical descriptors. Second, the sub-volumes (partitioned based on individual constituents) of such reconstructed 3D structures were fed into the NASA Multiscale Analysis Tool (NASMAT) to obtain homogenized properties of the cement. A semi-automated Python script was developed to complete the workflow.  Owing to the high computational demand, the analyses were carried out in NASA Advanced Supercomputing (NAS) servers.

Phase‑discerned ISS and ground BSE/SEM images were segmented and reconstructed into 3D volumes using a deep learning microstructure framework; these Representative Volume Elements (RVEs) were then analyzed with NASA’s Multiscale Analysis Tool (NASMAT) to homogenize and predict effective properties. Reconstruction quality was validated against statistical descriptors and micro‑CT data, and the modeling spans length‑scale partitioning to capture porous, multiphase behavior.
The experimental basis originated from the MICS investigation (PSI‑84 in the database), which conducted controlled ISS/ground hydration in sealed Burst Pouches, keeping temperature/pressure/humidity constant so gravity is the sole variable, followed by porosimetry, TGA, XRD, EDS/EMPA, and image analysis to quantify phase fractions and pore structures that feed the modeling pipeline.

hypothesis.value: Consistent with the microgravity MICS investigation, the central hypothesis was that minimizing gravity‑driven transport (buoyancy, sedimentation, convection) yields a diffusion‑controlled hydration process in microgravity, producing more uniform phase distributions and distinct microstructures (e.g., higher porosity, altered portlandite morphology) relative to 1g; these differences are expected to translate into measurably different mechanical properties for µg‑hardened cement paste versus terrestrial cement. The grant tested this by quantifying microstructural features from flight/ground samples and propagating them through micromechanics to predict property deltas attributable to gravity effects.

research_impacts.value:
This research provides the first reference simulation data and a practical route to predict how cement (including regolith‑based mixes) behaves when fabricated in space, which can inform Artemis‑aligned or other space-based habitat concepts and construction logistics where transporting bulk materials is prohibitive.
On Earth, the deep-learning-assisted reconstruction and micromechanics workflow developed can be applied to other multiphase materials, enabling materials-by-design even when only a limited samples are available. By clarifying how processing conditions in microgravity affect cement structure and performance, such as the ~70% porosity and plate-like portlandite observed in ISS samples, this work improves predictive models for optimizing mix designs and curing conditions in constrained environments. These advances also benefit low-resource or extreme-environment construction on Earth and contribute more broadly to the ICME community.

title.value: Investigating the Structure of Paramagnetic Aggregates from Colloidal Emulsions - 4

objectives.value: The overall objective of the InSPACE-4 investigation was to study the effects of particle shape and toggle duty cycle on the phase separation kinetics of particles in toggled fields. Three specific objectives include: (1) investigation of phase separation kinetics of anisotropic particles in toggled fields, (2) study the effect of toggle duty-cycle on the phase diagram, and (3) perform concurrent ground-based self-assembly experiments using the same magnetic colloids and extend the work to dielectric (insulating) particles driven by toggled alternating current (AC) electric fields.Concurrent ground-based experiments help translate International Space Station (ISS) discoveries to Earth-based manufacture by providing additional insights into the structure of equilibrated phases.

approach.value: This ISS investigation was conducted using  magnetic prolate ellipsoids with aspect ratios ranging from 2:1 to 4:1. Experiments involving spheres was also be conducted for comparison purposes. The sample material consisted of randomly oriented nano Fe3O4 coated polymer beads within a fluid filled vial, creating a magnetorheological fluid (MR). The vials were subjected to a pulsed magnetic field, which created a configuration of three-dimensional structures.The particle orientation was determined from birefringence measurements using crossed polarizers. The effects of particle shape, anisotropy, and magnetic field toggling frequency on the phase separation of particles was examined. Relatively short duration, ground-based experiments was conducted using the same magnetic particles to provide additional details about structure formation from particle-level to mesoscale structure.

hypothesis.value: Due to their anisotropic dynamics and interactions, investigators hypothesize that particle shape, in particular anisotropy (having different physical properties along different molecular axes), affects the phase separation kinetics of suspensions in toggled fields. Theoretical and simulation results suggesting that dynamic self-assembly can access a broad range of states analogous to equilibrium phases, even metastable ones, was also tested.

research_impacts.value: Discoveries from this work could lead to advanced materials for space applications such as better thermal shields, protection from micrometeorites, materials for energy production, energy-transfer devices, control systems and new mechanical actuators and sensors for robotic and human missions. This investigation helps advance the manufacture of next-generation nanomaterials for applications on Earth such as thermal shields, sound damping devices, shock absorbers, camouflage, medical diagnostic and environmental sensors, display technologies and advanced coatings. The technology also is expanding into larger-scale applications such as building foundation stabilizers for areas prone to earthquakes.

title.value: The origin of fragility in high-temperature oxide liquids - towards fabrication of novel non-equilibrium oxides

objectives.value:
This project investigated the high-temperature thermophysical properties of molten metal oxides, with a particular focus on molten titanates. These property measurements were used to establish correlations with atomic structure and glass formation.

The research exploits the unique capabilities in microgravity to measure the thermophysical properties – density, thermal expansion coefficient, viscosity and surface tension – over a wide temperature range. Samples, including glasses, were recovered after melt processing in microgravity for ground-based analysis and comparison with materials made on Earth. The work underpins development of a materials property-structure data set that can help in development of new materials and in meeting requirements of material utilization, processing in space, and exploration.

approach.value:
Density, thermal expansion, viscosity, and surface tension of molten oxides were measured using the Electrostatic Levitation Furnace (ELF) onboard the ISS. Measurements included silhouette imaging and drop oscillation over a wide range of temperatures, including deep supercooling.

Recovered samples included glasses and polycrystalline materials, which were characterized post-flight using a combination of X-ray scattering, neutron scattering, X-ray tomography, Raman spectroscopy, calorimetry, and electron microscopy. Space-made glasses were compared with terrestrial analogues to investigate how changes in fluid transport may influence structure and properties.

hypothesis.value: Glasses are inherently non-equilibrium materials. Their structure and properties depend directly on the processing route used to form them. Because gravity affects fluid convection, glass formation and resulting structure may differ between different gravity conditions. We hypothesize that the superior control of fluid and thermal transport possible in microgravity will enable improved glass forming ability via melt quenching in containerless conditions, particularly for highly fragile liquid oxides. We hypothesize that the differences in thermal history - between microgravity and Earth-based processing - will manifest as differences in structure and thermodynamic properties.

research_impacts.value:
This project advances the understanding of oxide melt properties, atomic structure, and glass formation. This builds a foundation for the development of new functional glasses and related technologies, with applications on Earth and in space for exploration and utilization of local resources.

The project was successful on several fronts:
1.	Microgravity experiments enabled melting, drop imaging, drop oscillation and measurements of properties of approximately 30 samples.
2.	First experiments in ELF that used melt processing to make and recover glass in space.
3.	First publications that compare the structure of glasses made in microgravity vs. terrestrially.
4.	First demonstration of laser action in a titanate-network glass and of a glass made by containerless processing.
5.	Results were analyzed in collaboration with a variety of researchers leading to 12 peer-reviewed publications and more than 20 presentations.
6.	Two patents are pending based on results of the work. These have a high impact on glass materials processing in space and development of new glass products both on-Earth and in reduced gravity.
7.	The project met all of the stated goals: perform basic research in microgravity, develop applied knowledge to make new materials, build collaborations to advance the field, and establish the basis for new glass materials products made in reduced gravity.
8.	The results are relevant to the applied research mission of NASA's Biological and Physical Sciences (BPS) to enable space exploration and utilize materials based on natural resources that are available in space.
9.	Developed and fostered a productive international collaboration.

title.value: Aerosol Sampling Experiment

objectives.value:
Aerosols are small particles suspended in the air, and in Earth’s atmosphere, aerosols include soot, dust, pollen and a wide range of other natural and human-made materials. Smoke does not rise and dust does not settle in microgravity the way they do on Earth, causing aerosols to behave differently and pose hazards for crew members breathing the air. The Aerosol Sampling Experiment (ASE) collects airborne particles in the International Space Station’s (ISS) cabin air, and returns them to Earth for scientists to study.

The objectives of ASE were:
1- Characterize airborne particulate matter aboard the ISS to assess air quality for crew health and hardware longevity.
2- Identify particle sources (e.g., human skin, equipment wear, biological contaminants) in the spacecraft environment.
3- Improve understanding of particle transport and accumulation in microgravity conditions.
4- Support design of future spacecraft air filtration systems, ensuring they are appropriately targeted for actual airborne particle profiles.

approach.value: The ASE approach involved passive aerosol sampling in multiple ISS modules using filters placed in air ducts and cabin areas (especially near high-traffic zones and vents) by deploying commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) samplers for long-duration exposure (3 months–1 year).  The sampled filters were returned to Earth for ground-based analysis using: 1- Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM), 2- Energy-Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDS) and 3- Gravimetric analysis. The ISS samples were compared to terrestrial cleanroom and indoor environments to assess relative cleanliness and particle source uniqueness.  Data collected was cross-referenced with previous ISS air monitoring efforts (e.g., TOCA, CCAA) to inform models of contaminant accumulation and mitigation.

hypothesis.value: Airborne particulate matter aboard the ISS exhibits a different size distribution, composition, and transport behavior in microgravity compared to Earth-based environments, and that particles from crew activity and hardware wear contribute significantly to the aerosol burden as well as the assumption that microgravity reduces sedimentation, allowing finer particles to stay suspended longer and accumulate in regions not typically affected by gravity-based settling on Earth.

research_impacts.value: Crew members on the ISS are breathing more or less the same fixed volume of air that has been on the ISS for years. There is no chance to get ‘fresh air’ as we do on Earth, but an advanced air revitalization system processes and cleans the air continuously. Crew members in space have complained of allergies and nose and eye irritation, which suggests the ISS cabin air has a high concentration of tiny particles that can be inhaled. The ISS filtration system is designed to remove these particles, but researchers have no way to verify the efficiency or cleanliness of the air. This investigation generates new data to characterize the quality of the air on the ISS, in terms of particles. Future space travelers may benefit from this data, as they can be used in the design and selection of particle detectors appropriate for low gravity. Long-term manned space missions need aerosol measurement capability to ensure crew health and comfort
