title.value: Structure and Properties of Pb-Sn and Pb-free Sn-Ag-Cu Solders Produced in Terrestrial vs. Microgravity Environments under Extremes of Elevated and Cryo Temperatures

subresearch_area.value: Microstructural Characterization, Terrestrial vs Microgravity Effects, Solder Joints

objectives.value: This study addresses the reliability of solder joints in space by pursuing two principal objectives: (1) Characterization of solder-joint formation under microgravity conditions aboard the International Space Station, specifically examining the impact of suppressed convective flow and buoyancy on 40Pb-60Sn alloys utilized in the In-Space Soldering Investigation (ISSI). (2) Evaluation of the solder’s material and mechanical properties under extreme thermal environments, including elevated and cryogenic temperature exposures characteristic of spaceflight conditions.

approach.value:
The study examined three distinct solder alloys: the ISSI lead-based (40Pb-60Sn) composition, an off-eutectic 50Pb-50Sn formulation, and a lead-free alloy consisting of 95.5Sn-3.8Ag-0.7Cu.
Microstructural characterization was performed on four solder specimens processed in microgravity from the ISSI investigation, one terrestrial ISSI solder, and a freshly fabricated terrestrial 40wt%Pb-60wt%Sn sample. These analyses elucidated the role of suppressed buoyancy and natural convection in void formation within microgravity environments. Evidence of void-induced Marangoni convection influencing microstructure development was demonstrated using wire-feed solder processed in space. The micromechanical response of solders fabricated under both terrestrial and microgravity conditions was further evaluated across a broad thermal range (–157ºC to +121ºC), simulating the conditions encountered externally on the International Space Station. Investigations under cryogenic conditions focused on the β-to-α phase transformation in Sn below 13ºC, examining associated volumetric expansion, internal stress evolution, and the ductile-to-brittle transition phenomena observed in Sn-based alloys. At ambient temperature, the influence of accelerated aging on both microstructural stability and mechanical performance was assessed.

hypothesis.value: In microgravity environments, fluid dynamics are markedly constrained, predominantly governed by solidification-induced volumetric changes, thermally driven density gradients, and Marangoni convection. This suppression of fluid motion results in diminished mixing, causing voids and gas bubbles to remain entrapped within the solder joint during the solidification process. Such internal porosity critically impairs the solder’s thermal and electrical conductivity, while also compromising the mechanical robustness of the joint. To advance the feasibility of extended space missions, this study seeks to elucidate the fundamental mechanisms, observable phenomena, and process parameters that influence the structural and functional integrity of solder joints fabricated under terrestrial and microgravity conditions.

research_impacts.value:
The research presented in this project offers significant contributions across multiple space exploration initiatives:

(i) The project objectives are closely aligned with ongoing NASA initiatives focused on metal joining techniques in reduced gravity environments. The three solder alloys investigated—selected in collaboration with NASA partners, underscoring the relevance of the study to future space exploration efforts, (ii) The findings are expected to inform the design of future experiments responsive to forthcoming NASA proposal calls, including those associated with the Artemis program, which aims to return humans to the lunar surface, (iii) The insights gained into microgravity fluid behavior and surface tension variation can be extended to a broad range of spaceflight-enabling technologies, such as boiling, heat transfer, combustion, welding, brazing, and soldering. This research enhances the understanding of gravity-driven separation processes—such as gas bubble removal—that must be accomplished via alternative mechanisms in microgravity conditions. (iv) The gravity-level-specific protocols (GLSPs) developed for various soldering configurations serve as practical guidance for future investigations into metal joining techniques under reduced gravity. These protocols may be adopted by scientists and flight personnel for welding, brazing, and soldering applications in spaceflight environments.

title.value: Colloidal gels:  Aging in microgravity, Structure of highly polydisperse gels

objectives.value:
Data are from two projects:  one related to aging, one related to polydispersity.  The first project has data under folders with a name containing AGING.  The second has data under folders with a name containing POLYDISPERSE.

-------

Project 1: Objectives specific to aging of colloid gels
•Quantify coarsening of colloidal gels under microgravity conditions.
•Quantify changes in thermal fluctuations of colloidal gels under microgravity conditions.
•Understand aging of colloidal gels over time scales range from seconds to tens of hours.

Project 2: Objectives related to structure of polydisperse colloidal gels
•Measure fractal dimension of polydisperse colloidal gels (on Earth)
•Understand how particle size relates to contact number
•Quantify tetrahedral structures, and how particle size influences tetrahedral structure in colloidal gels

approach.value:
Project 1: We studied colloidal gels using the data from the Advanced Colloids Experiment-Microscopy-1 (ACE-M1) experiments. Colloidal gels are formed from sticky micron-sized solid particles in a liquid, where over time the particles stick together and form random clumps that eventually bridge across the entire sample chamber in tangled networks. The ACE-M1 data set consists of a large number of optical microscopy movies of colloidal gels. In microgravity, these gels are long-lived, rather than collapsing under their own weight as happens in ground-based experiments. We have analyzed these microscopy movies using particle tracking, studying the visible thermal fluctuations and the gel structure as it evolves over time. Some gels have thick aggregated regions, while others have more tenuous gel strands and free particles. We show that the structure and dynamics change over the several-day period of each experiment.

Project 2: In a second project, we did ground-based experiments to study the structure of colloidal gels composed of polydisperse particles.  In particular, we used confocal microscopy to image colloidal gels formed from highly polydisperse particles. We suspended our polydisperse particles in a density matched solvent, and let the particles spontaneously aggregate through the van der Waals force. The largest particles were more than 15 times the size of the smallest particles.  As expected, larger particles have more nearest neighbors than small ones.  This leads to an over-representation of large particles in tetrahedral structures where four particles are mutually nearest neighbors, showing that large particles help provide rigidity to the gel structure.  The tetrahedral structures also suggest that particles are able to rearrange somewhat during the gelation process, until their motion is stabilized by the multiple contacts with their neighbors.

hypothesis.value:
Project 1:  Colloidal gels in microgravity conditions will coarsen over time, and their thermal fluctuations will diminish over time as the gel gets coarser; the coarsening will continue indefinitely because gravitational collapse will not be possible.

Project 2:  Large particles play significant roles in highly polydisperse colloidal gels, as they serve as highly connected nodes in the structure.

research_impacts.value: This research helps us understand the technical challenge of keeping particles dispersed in a colloidal suspension.  A gel is one way to prevent particles from settling, although the long-time behavior of a gel is challenging to study under Earth gravity.

title.value: Testing Analytical and Numerical Models in Phase Coarsening using NASA Physical Sciences Informatics System

objectives.value:
NASA has supported “coarsening in solid–liquid mixtures” (CSLM) experiments, performed in microgravity on the International Space Station (ISS), with greatly reduced sedimentation rate in partially molten alloys. CSLM experimental data are stored in NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI). Microgravity experiments offer a unique opportunity to test existing numerical modeling and theories of phase coarsening.

The objective of this research is to test existing numerical modeling methods for simulation of the microstructure evolution that occurs during phase coarsening, using experimental data for Sn-Pb mixtures currently held in PSI.

Results from this research can be found in the following publications:
Wang, K.G., Glicksman, M.E. Testing Numerical Modeling of Phase Coarsening by Microgravity Experiments. JOM 69, 2825–2830 (2017). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11837-017-2553-x

approach.value: (1) use data archived in NASA's PSI system from the Coarsening in Solid-Liquid Mixtures (CSLM) microgravity experiments to determine mean and maximum particle sizes in each sample processed through the CSLM microgravity experiments; (2) apply a two-dimensional (2-D) phase-field simulation code to allow simulation and evolution of initial microstructures that were observed in the CSLM experiments for Sn-Pb solid-liquid phase mixtures, and which provide input data for our phase-field code to numerically evolve coarsened microstructures over time; (3) calculate particle size distributions (PSDs) from the prior NASA CSLM experiments, our phase-field and multiparticle diffusion simulations, and from diffusion screening theory.

hypothesis.value: Phase-field and multiparticle diffusion numerical methods can be applied to simulate the evolution of the microstructure during phase coarsening, delivering accurate statistical physical quantities such as the particle size distribution (PSD). Phase-field modeling can adequately capture the complexity of the microstructures developed during phase coarsening at large volume fraction. In contrast, multiparticle diffusion modeling can track the evolution of microstructures consisting of nearly spherical particles that develop during phase coarsening at lower volume fraction.

research_impacts.value: The contributions from our research activities improved the understanding of fundamental materials phenomena, i.e., phase coarsening. We advanced the state of the art in both theory and simulation. Better understanding of two-phase microstructures will help engineers improve process designs in economically important areas, including liquid-phase sintering for the production of hard tool materials. The theory and simulation tools developed herein that are tested by microgravity experiments, will provide technical pointers for the improvement of important processes, microstructures, and materials properties. The improved knowledge of microstructure evolution in this project will have significant impact on alloy design and service-life strategies for alloy materials. The theory and simulation tools developed will provide guidance toward exploring the structure and properties of alloys. Finally, the theoretical and computational tools will save money and time for alloy modification.

title.value: Coupled Growth in Hypermonotectics

objectives.value: The overall objective of the Coupled Growth in Hypermonotectics is to understand the fundamental physics controlling solidification in immiscible alloy systems. Specific experimental goals were (1) to show that production of an aligned fibrous microstructure is possible in hypermonotectic alloys by achieving interfacial stability and steady state coupled growth through microgravity processing, (2) to determine the influence of alloy composition and growth velocity on microstructure, and (3) to determine the growth velocity and composition range over which interface stability is possible in a hypermonotectic alloy system.

approach.value:
The CGH experiment investigation flew aboard the Life and Microgravity Spacelab (LMS) mission during the summer of 1996. Processing conditions
were controlled in an attempt to force the production of an aligned fibrous phase in the microstructure of processed samples. The Advanced Gradient Heating Facility (AGHF) was used to directionally solidify the immiscible alloys. Aluminum (Al)-Indium (In) alloys were studied and specialized aluminum nitride (AlN) ampoules were used in order to control several undesirable effects that are sometimes observed during low gravity processing. Three alloy compositions, namely 17.3 weight % In monotectic, and 18.5 and 19.7 weight percent In hypermonotectic alloys were processed during this mission. A thermal gradient of 67 C/cm was achieved and all flight samples were processes at a translation velocity of 1 micrometer/s. Ground based control samples were subsequently processed under conditions identical to those of two of the flight samples in order to allow a direct comparison of the results.

hypothesis.value: This investigation aimed to answer fundamental unanswered questions concerning solidification of immiscible alloys, namely: (a) is it possible to solidify a hypermonotectic alloy under steady state interfacially stable conditions to produce a fibrous microstructure, (b) can a simple supercooling approach predict stability limits, (c) does extensive diffusion in the liquid phases result in morphological effects not observed in eutectic systems, and (d) what role does surface tension driven flow play at the solidification front.

research_impacts.value: Many alloys in immiscible systems show great promise for potential applications in areas that include superconductors, magnetic materials, catalysts, and electrical contacts. For example, some immiscible alloys may be used to produce filters that can remove micron-sized particles for medical applications. Other alloys are expected to exhibit superconducting characteristics or have unusual magnetic properties.

title.value: Plant Water Management

objectives.value:
The primary objectives of the Plant Water Management (PWM) experiments were to:

a) Experimentally characterize and validate the use of passive capillary and  geometric control for plant watering in microgravity.
The research quantified the stability limits of capillary-driven flow under varying conditions, evaluated aeration and bubble management performance within root-zone analogs, and assessed start-up, shutdown, and drainage behaviors of the fluidic system on orbit and also correlated observed flow regimes and saturation levels with computational capillary flow models to improve predictive design tools for reduced-gravity systems.
b) Advance the PWM technology toward higher Technology Readiness Levels (TRL), demonstrating reliable, scalable configurations for integration into future space-based plant growth habitats.
The resulting data and models informed the design of next-generation, low-mass, low-power life-support and food-production systems for long-duration missions on the Moon, Mars, and beyond.

approach.value: PWM employed passive capillary-based fluidic systems to deliver water and nutrients to plant root zones under microgravity aboard the ISS. Growth modules were designed with controlled channel geometries and surface-wetting properties to direct liquid flow, manage gas-liquid separation, and maintain root-zone aeration. Both hydroponic and soil-based configurations were tested to evaluate performance across different growth media. Measurements included monitoring liquid distribution, root-zone moisture levels, aeration efficiency, and bubble formation, alongside comparing observations to predictive capillary flow models. By systematically varying system geometry, wetting conditions, and operational parameters, the experiments defined design guidelines for robust, low-maintenance plant growth systems for space and analogous terrestrial applications.

hypothesis.value: This research was based on the hypothesis that, in microgravity where gravity-driven fluid behavior is absent, capillary forces, surface tension, and geometric design could provide reliable water and nutrient delivery to plant root zones. Passive physical mechanisms replaced gravity in distributing and reclaiming fluids within the growth systems. Surface-wetting characteristics and channel geometry were designed to maintain root-zone hydration, facilitate aeration, and manage liquid–gas separation without pumps or active components. These mechanisms sustained water availability and oxygen exchange, preventing oversaturation or desiccation. The approach demonstrated that passive capillary systems could support consistent, low-maintenance plant watering and aeration in reduced-gravity environments.

research_impacts.value:
Demonstrating passive fluid management in plant growth systems is enabling reliable water and nutrient delivery in microgravity, supporting long-duration space missions.
Advancing capillary-based irrigation is reducing system mass, complexity, and power requirements. In relation to agriculture on Earth, results from this research are improving precision irrigation, conserving water, and enhancing root-zone aeration in hydroponic and soil systems. Generating validated models of capillary-driven flow is guiding efficient, resilient plant growth technologies. Supporting scalable, low-maintenance systems is fostering innovations in both space life-support and sustainable food production on Earth.

title.value: Advanced Colloids Experiment-Temperature 4

objectives.value:
Original Objective: The ACE-T4 experiments were designed to explore the disorder-induced transformation between a crystal and a glass. The experiments introduced disorder by added colloidal dopants into the samples; these dopants introduce structural frustration into the crystals which, in turn, can transform the crystals into disordered solids (polycrystalline) and glasses with novel mechanical properties. The experiments varied the concentration and character of particle dopants in three-dimensional colloidal crystals and employed direct visualization of an evolving crystal microstructure and dynamics in microgravity to derive fundamental insight into the nature of the transition and the glasses formed.

Revised Objective: Before the ACE-T4 experiment on the International Space Station (ISS) was conducted, the master hard disk controlling the Light Microscopy Module (LMM) failed and delayed starting this experiment by many months. This extended delay had a detrimental effect on the samples that  resulted in the gelation of the samples before the experiment began. The originally planned experiments were no longer possible due to gelation, but the ACE-T4 experiment based on the changed samples (gels) provided qualitatively different insights into the behavior of 3D colloidal gels over a range of temperatures and temperature gradients. Some effects were visible with LMM and provide an opportunity to study the microstructure, dynamics, and stresses in gels that can lead to microcracks, an important problem that, for example, could affect 3D printer inks.

approach.value: The ACE-T4 experiment used confocal microscopy to observe the gels over a range of particle packing-fractions (temperatures), using pure, monodisperse poly(N -isopropylacrylamide) (pNIPA) particles in one sample, and then mixtures of pNIPAM particles with different amounts of particle dopants in five other samples. All of the samples formed gels. There was no crystallization in any sample . The data obtained permits the study of 3D gels with and without dopants as a function of temperature; the temperature changes vary the particle size and thus properties of the gels. In addition to the revised ACE-T4 experiment, ground-based soft matter research was completed and published.

hypothesis.value: The ACE-T4 experiments were intended to explore the transformation between a crystal and a glass by varying the density and character of particle dopants in three dimensional colloidal crystals. The original hypothesis stated that ''dopants introduce structural frustration into the crystals which, in turn, can transform the crystals into disordered (polycrystalline) solids and glasses with novel mechanical properties. Direct visualization of the evolving crystal microstructure and dynamics in microgravity will provide fundamental insight into the nature of glasses and into processes such as nucleation and melting.''

research_impacts.value: By frustrating their structural order, the transition from ordered (crystal) to disordered (glassy) materials can alter the macroscopic behavior of ordered materials. Moreover, these experiments could also provide fundamental insight into the nature of nucleation, aging, and melting in materials with varying degrees of order. This information could benefit observation and synthesis of new colloidal materials (e.g. g., meta and photonic materials) for many applications ranging from color control to random laser.

title.value: Validation of a CFD Model for Gas-Liquid Flows in Packed Bed Reactors to Enable Thermo-Fluid Analysis in Microgravity

objectives.value:
1. Develop and validate computational models for gas-liquid two-phase flow in porous media under microgravity using the  PBRE (Packed Bed Reactor Experiment) flight data available in Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI).
2. Understand capillary-dominated fluid dynamics in low-gravity environments where traditional gravity-driven models fail.
3. Advance CFD tools to support the design and scale-up of life support and thermal control systems for spacecraft, space stations, and lunar/Martian habitats.

approach.value:
In this grant, our approach combined high-fidelity simulations with reduced-order modeling to better understand and predict two-phase gas-liquid flows through packed bed reactors in microgravity. We began by developing interface-resolved CFD simulations using the Volume of Fluid (VOF) method to capture detailed bubble dynamics in a representative volume of the reactor. These simulations were validated using PBRE imagery and pressure data available in PSI.

To address scale-up and improve computational efficiency, we also developed a two-fluid model (TFM), which treats the gas and liquid phases as interpenetrating continua rather than tracking individual interfaces. We calibrated the drag closure in this model using PBRE data, allowing us to predict pressure drop behavior across different flow regimes. By combining detailed CFD with a validated TFM, we created a versatile modeling framework that supports the design of life support and thermal systems for future space missions.

Published or archived data sets:
   – Pranay P. Nagrani; Amy M. Marconnet; Ivan C. Christov (2023). Simulations, data, and scripts for Hydrodynamics of bubble flow through a porous medium with applications to packed bed reactors. Purdue University Research Repository. doi:10.4231/8AJD-2483.
 – Pranay P. Nagrani; Amy M. Marconnet; Ivan C. Christov (2024). Simulations, data, and scripts for Correlations for the interphase drag in the two-fluid model of gas-liquid flows through packed-bed reactors.  Purdue University Research Repository. doi:10.4231/VHB3-EN13.

hypothesis.value: not_reported

research_impacts.value:
In space, fluid behavior becomes unpredictable. This grant developed and validated advanced computational models using real data from microgravity experiments to improve our understanding of how gas and liquid mixtures flow through packed bed reactors in space systems. This research can enable the design of more reliable and scalable systems for future missions to the Moon and Mars.

On Earth, the same fluid dynamics apply to industries like chemical processing, wastewater treatment, and energy systems. The resulting models and insights from this research can improve efficiency and reduce costs in these applications.

microgravity.sentence: Validation of a CFD Model for Gas-Liquid Flows in Packed Bed Reactors to Enable Thermo-Fluid Analysis in Microgravity

Develop and validate computational models for gas-liquid two-phase flow in porous media under microgravity using the PBRE (Packed Bed Reactor Experiment) flight data available in Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI).
Understand capillary-dominated fluid dynamics in low-gravity environments where traditional gravity-driven models fail.
In this grant, our approach combined high-fidelity simulations with reduced-order modeling to better understand and predict two-phase gas-liquid flows through packed bed reactors in microgravity.

This grant developed and validated advanced computational models using real data from microgravity experiments to improve our understanding of how gas and liquid mixtures flow through packed bed reactors in space systems.

title.value: Particle Engulfment and Pushing By Solidifying Interfaces

approach.value:
The experimental approach was to perform directional solidification experiments with a pure metal, aluminum, doped with low
volume fraction of insoluble particles, ZrO2. These experiments were carried out during the Life and Microgravity Science (LMS) mission on board the space shuttle Columbia. In addition, transparent organic matrices such as succinonitrile and biphenyl doped with polystryrene particles or glass beads were used to observe the interaction between the particle and solidification interface in real time. The experiments with the organic matrices were performed during the United States Microgravity Payload 4 (USMP-4) mission also on board the space shuttle Columbia. Planar interfaces were produced through appropriate manipulation of the solidification variables, so that a clear pushing/engulfment transition (PET) of the particles could be determined. Both ground and microgravity experiments were conducted.
Recognizing that the interaction between the particle and the solidification front is not completely a steady state process, a dynamic non-steady-state model was developed based on the fact that a particle, initially at rest, must have an accelerated motion in order to reach the steady-state velocity, which is the solidification velocity. To account for the solutal fields in alloys a 2D FDM fixed Cartesian grid numerical model was also developed. The models were validated using benchmark microgravity and terrestrial data.

hypothesis.value: During solidification of metal-insoluble particles systems the particles interact with the solidification front. The solutal and thermal field, as well as fluid motion at the solid-liquid interface (SLI) will influence both interface morphology and the particle/interface interaction itself. This investigation hypothesizes that based on the nature of interaction and balance of forces acting on the particle there is a critical SLI velocity below which particles are pushed ahead of the advancing interface, and above which particle engulfment occurs. For planar SLI the critical velocity results from the forces acting on the particle. These forces include particle-SLI interaction force, drag force on the particle, gravitational force, Saffman force, and Magnus force. The last three are strongly affected by the level of gravitational acceleration.

research_impacts.value: A fundamental understanding of the phenomena associated with particle/interface interaction during solidification will permit the development of novel techniques for processing of particulate metal matrix composites through melting and solidification. Similar concepts apply to inclusion management in casting alloys. As for most other metallurgical applications it is desired to avoid inclusion segregation at grain boundaries. Results of this research can be extrapolated straightforward to “clean steel” technology. Another interesting application of particle pushing is in the processing of single crystals ceramic where strong flux pinning particles are desired to be homogeneously incorporated in the superconducting crystal. Insights from this investigation can also be applied to the field of cryobiology where the study of the interaction of cells (yeast cells, red blood cells) with ice crystals when freezing aqueous solutions makes it possible to investigate the mechanism of the mechanical destruction of biological structures by ice crystals on freezing biological materials. In addition, this investigation can be extended to the field of frost heaving of soils that can be reduced to the behavior of soil particles (i.e. clay) in a water/ice matrix.

microgravity.sentence: The major scientific objectives of this investigation were as follows: · to enhance the fundamental understanding of dynamics of insoluble particles at the solid-liquid interface; · to obtain experimental data for the critical velocity of particle engulfment in a convection-free environment; · to validate present theoretical models; · to improve the understanding of physics associated with solidification of liquid metals - ceramic particles mixtures; · to investigate aspects of melt processing of particulate metal matrix composites in the unique microgravity environment which will yield some vital information for terrestrial applications; · to further develop the elements of the numerical model into a comprehensive model that takes into account convection effects.
These experiments were carried out during the Life and Microgravity Science (LMS) mission on board the space shuttle Columbia.
The experiments with the organic matrices were performed during the United States Microgravity Payload 4 (USMP-4) mission also on board the space shuttle Columbia.
Both ground and microgravity experiments were conducted.
The models were validated using benchmark microgravity and terrestrial data.

title.value: Advanced Colloids Experiment-Temperature 5

objectives.value: The overarching goal of the project was to gain a better fundamental understanding of the relationship between bijel morphology, rheology, mechanical stability, and processability through combined ground-based and microgravity experiments and theoretical calculations.

approach.value: Mixtures of propylene glycol/nitroethane (PG/NE) at their critical composition were prepared. Partially hydrophobic silica particles were suspended in the PG/NE mixture and the suspensions were filled in different cuvettes. On orbit, these cuvettes were heated to 25C, mixed in-situ, and then quenched from 25C to 0C. Following the quench, an imaging protocol was used to collect a stack of 100 images in the Z direction at a spacing of 5 mm.

hypothesis.value: This investigation hypothesizes that interparticle interactions have a profound impact on the rheology of bijel particulate suspensions and attempts to answer the fundamental scientific question as to how the various forces at the colloidal scale are affected by Marangoni convection in microgravity. The nature of interparticle interactions and its impact on rheology has profound implications for the processability of bijels and the ability to transform them into functional materials.

research_impacts.value:
The ability to design and fabricate the unique 3-dimensional bijel structures opens a wide spectrum of new structures for applications that can benefit from synthesis of hierarchically
porous monoliths and composites with a spinodal-like microstructure in which every constituent phase is naturally continuous throughout the entire sample volume. This type of tailored porous
microstructures can improve the physical properties and performance of materials used in a number of space and terrestrial applications. Space exploration applications include improved energy
storage batteries and fuel cells, and catalytic microreactors for lower mass and volume designs in spacecraft life support and ISRU systems. There is a diverse array of potential terrestrial applications in electrochemical energy conversion and storage, tissue engineering, sensing, microstructured composites with optimized mechanical properties for MEMS, microfluidic heat exchangers and catalytic reformers, separations.
